paragraphs.text: PROLOGUE.

A PROFESSION OF FAITH AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY THAT BY GOD'S WILL ALONE SOME ARE DRAWN TO LIFE AND OTHERS PRESSED DOWN INTO DEATH, AND WHO THEREBY ASSERT FATE WITH THE PAGANS ON THE ONE HAND AND DENY FREE WILL WITH THE MANICHAEANS ON THE OTHER.
TO THE MOST BLESSED AND MOST REVEREND LORD, POPE LEONTIUS, FAUSTUS.

Blessed Pope Leontius, when in your pastoral care you assembled a council of the chief bishops to condemn the error of predestination, you did a service to all the churches of Gaul. But when you entrusted to weak shoulders the labor and the care of setting in order what you had so learnedly set forth in public conference, you took too little thought, I think, for so great a matter, and too little for your own holy reputation: you laid on me the burden of charity's judgment, and on yourselves the risk of your choice. Since, then, you recognize that your own person also labors under the burden laid upon us, you are pleading a common cause here if you stretch out a supporting hand to one whom you yourselves consider unequal to the task. He takes up the task of upholding grace fittingly and soundly who joins to it the obedience of labor as its servant, as a footman attends his patron or master and never leaves his side. If the one is without the other, either the master will appear without honor, having no servant, or the servant, forgetting his station, will take the master's place. This order will rightly be kept, then, between the one who helps and the one who strives along with him: the first holds dominion by full right, the second renders service in complete subjection. And the dignity of the one who commands will be increased if the diligence of the one who obeys is always at hand. Let the lowest be joined to the highest, and joined in such a way that they are subordinated, not made equal. Just as it is not fitting for a helmsman to lack his oarsman, a priest his minister, or an emperor his soldier, so grace must be bound to obedience, its nursling, in a service that cannot be severed. But Pelagius extols bare labor with excessive insistence, and in his madness foolishly believed and impiously preached that human weakness can suffice for itself without grace, trying to raise a tower of pride up to heaven. I have therefore judged it necessary to touch briefly on his blasphemies and refute them. Otherwise, when we assert that God's mercy must be merited by faith and works, someone who excludes the gift of labor, that is, the command of the One who commands, might apply our catholic statement to Pelagius's meaning, not knowing how to discern between them; having left the royal road and fallen to the right, he might think we were veering to the left; and while we speak of labor as the servant of grace, we might seem to have put a stumbling block before the feet of the blind. Whenever we mention works and labor, we shall use both the words and the meaning of the prophet, the apostle and the evangelists. If anyone presumes to oppose them, he will be trying not to tear down our inventions but beyond doubt to dissolve heavenly laws and undermine the foundations of the faith. We have extended our discussion of foreknowledge and predestination at somewhat greater length, so that what was thought obscure might be made plainer for slower readers. And let it not offend those who delight in the trappings of words that, content with the force of the testimonies, we have brought forth the light of truth without loftiness of style. After this little work had been subscribed by the Council of Arles, new errors were detected, and a synod at Lyons required that some things be added to it.
CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK.
I. That the view of Pelagius, who denied grace, must be demolished first.
II. Against Pelagius's objection in which he says that infants do not need baptism.

III. Against the claim that every man is saved by grace alone without any labor. Against the view which, by saying "one is predestined to death, another is predestined to life," in effect shuts off the hope of prayer.
IV. Where the works of the law are demolished and the works of grace commended.
V. On the saying: "By the grace of God I am what I am."
VI. How the saying is to be understood: "By grace," it says, "you have been saved through faith, and this not of yourselves."
VII. Against the claim that free will was taken away entirely.
VIII. How the weakness of free will is to be understood.
IX. How the saying is to be understood: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy," and also: "I came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance."
X. Against the claim that man's will is ready only for evil and not at all for good.
XI. Against the view which says that a vessel for dishonor cannot rise up to become a vessel for honor.
XII. Likewise, that willing and not willing have been entrusted to man's choice, toward the good as well as toward the evil.
XIII. Where the grace of God and the human will are shown by the testimonies to be joined together, and the empty calumny about infants is touched on in passing.
XIV. Against the claim that those who perish after baptism never truly believed in baptism at all.
XV. On the fall of the angel, and that the holy angels bear the likeness of God, against the persuasion of some.
XVI. That Christ died for all.
XVII. Against the claim that God hardens a man by force, so that he cannot come to salvation.
XVIII. That no one perishes by God's will.
BOOK ONE.
THAT THE VIEW OF PELAGIUS, WHO DENIED GRACE, MUST BE DEMOLISHED FIRST.

We are about to treat, with the Holy Spirit to enlighten us, of the grace of God and the frailty of free will, following the teachings of the gospel and the rules of the apostles. First, we believed, the blasphemies of Pelagius must be touched on in a brief and necessary discourse. They have long since been exposed by the faith of the Catholic Church, confounded by learning and trampled down by authority, but among the other abominations of his doctrine he tried, with damnable pride, to affirm that human labor can avail without grace. We shall therefore take care to bring his wicked views into the open, at least in part, so that every careful reader may know that it is one thing to join the service of labor to saving grace, and quite another to assert, out of sheer rashness of heart, bare labor without the patronage of grace.

This man, then, exalting human frailty too high and forgetting the fear of God, lost the soundness of his judgment. In preaching that freedom of choice is whole and unimpaired, he fell on one side, just as those fall on the other who assert that it was entirely emptied out. Here, then, twin errors wrestle with each other: one urges grace alone, the other labor alone, and both have abandoned the path and measure of truth. Different in the kind of sect but alike in impiety, they hiss with different zeal but with the spirit of one serpent. The one, the preacher of grace alone, at first sight hides its poison under the appearance of piety; the other, the champion of labor, at once displays its swollen tumor with shameless pride. This profession, urging labor alone, is detestable by its very title; that one, under a religious color, is more to be feared. This one betrays its sacrilege to the ears themselves; that one pours its venom into the inmost vitals almost before it is felt. Picture two rocks besetting a narrow strait, one sunk down into the deep, the other towering threateningly toward heaven. The one is plainly seen to be a danger to sailors; the other, unforeseen, causes shipwrecks no one sees coming. The one speaks of grace, the other of labor. The divine oracles confirm both. If you remove the dissenters and join together what they say, the full integrity of the faith will appear. But like rash oarsmen without a master they commit their sails to an unexplored sea; they do not know how to set their course and have no skill at the helm. So one is carried into the peril of Scylla on the ill-fated right, while the other heads for the abyss of Charybdis on the left. And if you ask what they ought to do in this situation: let them take on a helmsman before entrusting the ship to the waves, let them hold a middle course, and a favorable wind will bring both to harbor.

Let us see to what impiety we can liken or compare this twin error. Those who, having lost the light of discernment, presumed to assert that Christ the Lord is God alone, and those who presumed to assert that he is man alone, stumble alike on the rock of offense. Both excesses, not knowing how to keep distinctions and differences, incur almost equal guilt. Whoever says that Christ is man alone has denied the power of the Author; whoever says he is God alone has lost the mercy of the Redeemer. And so those who confess one substance in the Lord and Savior will be bound by this necessity: they are forced to say either that a mere man came down from heaven or that God alone was crucified. But it is not so. For God alone could not have felt death, nor could man alone have overcome it; therefore, by reason of the twofold substance, the man underwent death and God conquered it. If, then, you give each part its own properties and believe and assert that Christ is God and man together, it is just as if you join grace with labor and do not separate man's effort from God's help—yet in such a way that you mix no guilt of pride whatever into the devotion of the one who strives. For as much harm as there is in not laboring, so much danger is there in presuming on one's labor.

Pelagius says, then, that human nature is sufficient by itself to obtain salvation. This pestilent teacher affirms it as though the workmanship of our creation still remained unimpaired in its original state. I think that freedom of choice could not have sufficed by itself without the protection of grace even before the first transgression violated its privilege. How then can it now suffice by itself, when to its arrogance it is said, "Without me you can do nothing," and when the divine word is directed against its presumption: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain"? What is denied to pride without grace to accomplish is granted to humility with grace to fulfill.

Pelagius goes on to say that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he had sinned or not. But since the apostle says, "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death," you understand that if sin had not come first, death would not have followed, and the immortality that had been given would have endured. That immortality was plainly granted under a law set before him and conferred on a condition: if he did not proudly withdraw from obedience, he would remain eternal in glory. For when God had sanctioned the heavenly prohibition, saying, "On whatever day you eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall surely die," the ill-counseled presumption of that forbidden taste became an accidental occasion of death. "You shall surely die," he says. If the grace of the Giver conferred nothing, what is it that the displeasure of the One who condemned took away? Death, then—an alien evil that came from outside—is not the order of nature but the penalty of a sentence. "For," it says, "the Lord did not make death." The very envy of the enemy testifies that eternity had been entrusted to man: because, having been cast down himself, he begrudged man his immortality, he introduced the cause of death by saying, "On whatever day you eat of this tree, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods." Had he said only, "When you eat, you will be satisfied by the sweetness of the food," the transgression would have gone as far as the allurement of carnal desire. But since he set this as the goal of the transgression, saying, "You will be like gods," the fault of gluttony went as far as grasping at divinity, as far as the crime of high treason. So they were made "like gods": stripped of the gift of heavenly grace and thrust down from the summit of their blessed station. Thus the cunning serpent, cast out of heaven for the evil of pride, contrived from his own fall and lapse the machinery for overthrowing man, and deceived in the same way that he himself fell.

What else is to be understood in the very image of God in which man was created, if not the mark of everlastingness? You recognize that this everlastingness was not only never taken from the soul but is restored even to the body by the power of the resurrection. Do not doubt, therefore, that immortality was entrusted to man before the fault, since you see it given back even after the fall.

Pelagius asserts, then, that Adam would have died in any case, whether he sinned or not. This springs from the same perversity by which he denies original sin. For in striving to affirm that the necessity of death belonged to creation and not to transgression, he wants the origin of this debt to seem to have begun not with the servant but with the master, not with the one who scorned the command but with the Author, so that the law of death may be believed to come from God's ordinance and not from a crime. Is it then to be thought that this lamentable ruin was handed down upon the human race not by the transgressor but by the Creator? And where then is that saying: "But through the envy of the devil death entered the world"? Moreover, in denying original sin he removes altogether the reason for which the Redeemer came. Let us see whether this unhappy and lamentable condition began through the will of God or through the depravity of man. Hear what the trumpet of truth sounds: "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, so death passed to all men, in whom all sinned." By saying that Adam was made mortal, Pelagius places death in the first order of creation, whereas it is clear that it was imposed at the third stage, as punishment for transgression. For man is the work of God, sin the work of the devil, and death the penalty of sin. The apostle did not say, "Death is the will of God," but, "The wages of sin is death."

Let us look more carefully, then, at his tricks lurking in the depths. He attributes death to the Creator so that it cannot be recognized from what evil above all it takes its origin, and so that he may affirm the more freely that infants are not held by the bond of origin. In saying this he blasphemes with a double impiety: he shifts the odium of death onto the Author, and by denying the original bond he empties out the grace of the Restorer. So, in order to be able to assert that infants do not need baptism, he denied the universal sin; and having denied it, his error followed its course, so that he did not know whence death had arisen. What wonder if he does not recognize that tree by its fruits when he refused to know it by its root? He suppresses the cause of the wound and hides the sword by which the wound was inflicted. "The wages," it says, "of sin is death." Because he neglected to understand the prince of so great an evil, he did not know that the condition of death imposed on us follows sin as its attendant, as we said earlier: "The wages of sin is death." He who served as the devil's soldier received the pay that such work deserves; such were the wages he earned. Hence the vessel of election shows and preaches most clearly the reason for the redemption, saying: "For why, while we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly? For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous man." That is to say: if righteousness had abounded on earth, no remedy would have been sent from heaven. But the sickness of all demanded the coming of the one and only cure.

Since Pelagius is bound by such great chains of sacrilege, it is no wonder if he is handed over through a reprobate mind to manifold error, thinking that he can be saved by labor alone. Rightly does the divine word exert the force of its authority and rebuke against the presumption of such arrogance: "No one," it says, "comes to me unless the Father draws him," and again: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy." Whoever, with Pelagius, places his salvation in his own will and strength will rightly consider this said to himself. But there is certainly no need to raise this objection against one who does not presume on labor alone, but knows that God's daily mercy and constant grace must be implored for his efforts, and begs the Lord's help with unceasing, watchful prayer.
II. AGAINST PELAGIUS'S OBJECTION IN WHICH HE SAYS THAT INFANTS DO NOT NEED BAPTISM.

Pelagius also urges this point: if original sin is taken away by the gift of baptism, those born of two baptized parents ought to be free of this sin. "How," he says, "do they pass on to their offspring what they themselves did not have in them at all?" The answer to such people is easy: there are two births. From the one, sin is transmitted through the pleasure of the one who begets; by the other, sanctification is bestowed through the adoption of the One who regenerates. "How," he says, "do they pass on to their offspring what they themselves did not have in them at all?" What an irrational objection, and how full of wickedness! You will not have them pass on to their offspring what belongs to nature—that nature of which the apostle says, "You were by nature children of wrath"—and yet you will have them able to confer, as if from their own store, what belongs to grace. Rightly they cannot give as their own what they received from above and from outside. Most imprudently Pelagius believes that the purity of innocence is given to children through their parents. The second birth does not belong to the ministry of parents. He wants what is God's gift to be man's function, so that what clearly lies outside human substance should run through the posterity of men as though by some order of inheritance. But there is no doubt that original sin passes from parents, even baptized parents, to their children through the origin of the flesh, since we say daily with the prophet: "For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me"; just as the apostle also confirms that this incurable guilt passed from one man into all men.

But Pelagius says that there is no original sin, because the very desire to procreate comes from God. If you ask where this bond comes from that draws posterity along with it: beyond doubt, through the inflaming heat of accursed generation and through the alluring embrace of both parents. For since you see that he alone is immune from the original contagion who was conceived not of flesh but of the Spirit, not by a shameful passion but by a wondrous blessing, recognize that the cause of the original evil was born of the delight of conception and the vice of pleasure. That is also why this condition did not hold Adam and Eve liable in their own origin: their coming into being, too, owed nothing to the agency of two, and so knew no allurement in their birth and creation. But perhaps you ask why original sin was placed in conception. The beginning of the whole ruin was disobedience. Man was first exalted, and afterward humbled and confounded. "And because, when he was in honor, he did not understand, he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them." As long as humility kept its reverence in obedience to the Author, an unstained conscience did not feel nakedness. But when, intending to be God, he craved the taste of the deadly food and stretched his damnable desire to grasping at majesty, forgetful of the law and rebellious against the commands of the law, he was punished by the revolt of his own members; presuming to equality with his Lord, he lost mastery over his own body. Incontinence was born of pride. He showed what had been stricken in him when he covered his shameful parts. Pride went before; shame followed. He who aspired to divinity began to be the captive of lust.

But perhaps you will say: in arguing this, you are caught condemning marriage. Not so. The institution of marriage began with a blessing; generation contracted its corruption from the transgression. Between the gift of marriage, granted by the Creator while still in paradise, and its use, which began only outside paradise, sin stood in the middle. In generation and concupiscence, whatever the divine command established I praise; whatever human transgression added I reject. It is as if someone spattered the whiteness of a snowy garment with black filth: it is not the workmanship that displeases, but the stain. The garment has not lost its use, though it has lost its dignity. Generation would beyond doubt have been chaste and pure had hostile transgression not intervened. But the flesh, made over to the curse, defiled the undefiled marriage bed and through the spirit of pride corrupted a simple affection; and as it lost the privilege of immortality, so it lost the gift of purity. It is not the grace of marriage that is called into question, but the injury of obscene passion. It is not the gold that is blamed, but whatever base alloy the fraud of iniquity mixed into the pure gold—just as the author of wickedness infected with pestilent corruption the spirit of Pelagius himself, which God had created for better pursuits.
III. AGAINST THE CLAIM THAT EVERY MAN IS SAVED BY GRACE ALONE WITHOUT ANY LABOR.

Now we must come to those who, by asserting that grace is given to some and denied to others, have lost the gift of grace along with Pelagius. They say that for the worship and service of God, even after the saving gift of baptism, the obedience of devoted service is not required, but that grace alone, by itself, brings about human salvation. "Everything," they say, "belongs to grace alone." That could better be said by us; it fits our side better, since we confess that the benefits of grace extend not to a part of the human race but to the whole of it, yet in such a way that we judge human watchfulness and effort to be joined to it in all things. For whoever denies that the servant's labour and striving must be joined to grace takes away from man the duty of service. I do not know where or when a man ought to rest from work, or when he ought to be left to idleness, since even in paradise he was commanded to work. There, as we read, he was placed in order to work it and to keep it.
AGAINST THE VIEW WHICH, BY SAYING THAT ONE PERSON IS FOREORDAINED TO DEATH AND ANOTHER PREDESTINED TO LIFE, IN EFFECT SHUTS OFF THE HOPE OF PRAYER.

When they say, "Everything belongs to the grace of God," who would not bow with all the affection of his heart before so venerable a name? But when we answer, "Everything plainly belongs to grace, but the Creator and Redeemer offers it to all and presses it upon all for the salvation of all," they turn far from the path of piety and presume to reply: "The Saviour did not give it to all, because he did not die for all." At once, in what they say next, the man who was thought at first to be the champion of grace appears as its assailant. They hold up the name of grace to cover an abominable and blasphemous view. In this way they exclude the help of prayer on both sides. For what more can a man hope for whom grace has already made its own? And on the other side, what can a man not despair of whom a forceful foreordination has condemned? In the one there is no room for guilt; in the other there is no room for grace. Justice will be imperilled in both cases. The one who is taken up will be rewarded without the merit of faith; the one who is abandoned will be condemned without any crime of his own. In the one case salvation must be forced on a man who does not seek it; in the other it must be taken away from a man who labours for it.

But you say: "He ought to pray for this very reason, that he does not know which side he is on." Who would not think that a reasonable and wise reply? But what good will prayer do a man who is set, without any possibility of change, in one of these two conditions? For even if he does not know to which side he has been assigned, he does know that both sides are fixed and unchangeable. What does it matter that he does not yet know his place, if he knows with complete certainty that the right hand now admits no danger and the left no progress? But if so confused a belief still thinks prayer necessary, let it acknowledge without hesitation that, contrary to its own definition, a man can pass from salvation to perdition and from perdition to salvation. If, then, it does not think the practice of prayer should be abandoned, let it not exclude the effort of working. What is this? Do you judge that I ought to knock, and yet despair of the door being opened to me? Let it therefore do one or the other: either deny the fruit of prayer or do away with the law of a fixed perdition. So we see that this assertion, full of error, while it shuts off the reason for praying, begins from the light of grace, but its end runs down and fails in the darkness of sacrilege. Thus the devil, with the cunning of his ancient craft and his many-sided ingenuity, seasons the enticements of sin. So too poisoners are accustomed to act: they mix deadly juices of herbs, and when they are about to offer them to the unsuspecting in spiced wine or some other sweet drink, they arrange the taste with a counterfeit sweetness and hide the venom's bitterness by the deceit of sweetness. The first scent of the cup entices, but the hidden taste of the poison chokes. It is honey that rises to the lips, but gall that goes down into the bowels.

They say that, in either state of things, death claims the one group for itself and life protects the other. Since this is said by someone who affirms that one person is lost in his origin and another chosen in predestination, see where his wicked persuasion leads. For what else does he say than that neither needs the help of prayer? For to those already foreordained to life it will not be necessary, and to those assigned to death it can be of no use. In the one case it will be judged superfluous, in the other powerless. The one who is in the predestination of gain does not need the benefits of supplication; the one who is on the side of perdition does not receive them. But if he thinks care should be devoted to prayer, let him understand without hesitation that what threatens can be changed, according to the Gospel saying: "Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation"; and again: "Watch, therefore, praying at all times, that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man"; and again: "This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting." If prayer is not necessary, why did he himself, the one to whom we must pray, establish a form of prayer, and why did he pray? In the man, then, who flatters untaught ears by asserting grace alone, that prophetic saying will be fulfilled: "The wicked man does harm when he mingles with the righteous." At first the appearance of gold shows itself in its colour, but cheap lead is found to lie hidden within. As when an enemy suddenly appears beneath the outward dress of a fellow citizen he has counterfeited, or as when the cunning subtlety of the enemy transforms itself into an angel of light, so under the face of piety the evil of paganism will be hidden, and within the word "grace" a decree of fate. If, then, as they assert, one is assigned to life and another to perdition, then, as one of the saints said, we are born not to be judged but already judged, and on this view no fairness of judgement can stand. For if God gave nothing to his servant, what will he demand back from his servant?
IV. THE WORKS OF THE LAW ARE DESTROYED AND THOSE OF GRACE ARE COMMENDED; OR: AGAINST THE FACT THAT THEY MOST IGNORANTLY PUT FORWARD TESTIMONIES IN SUPPORT OF GRACE ALONE.

"We read," they say, "in Romans: 'For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God'; and again: 'Now to one who works, the reward is not reckoned as grace but as what is owed. But to one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness.'" They add also: "But if it is by grace, it is not by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace." To them we must answer that there are two kinds of works, one of which is set aside after the coming of the Lord, while the other is approved. For in saying, "But to one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness," he plainly puts faith before the works of the law. Nor shall we say that the testimonies of the apostles conflict and contradict one another, when another apostle says: "Faith without works is dead"; and again: "Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and tremble"; and again: "For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead." Nor will Paul himself, the teacher of the Gentiles, appear inconsistent or self-contradictory when he says: "In all things let us commend ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours"; and again: "Each will receive his own reward according to his own labour." To the inexperienced, the untaught, and those who resist the truth with an obstinate spirit, these things will seem to disagree. But according to the catholic rule, the works of the law, which are according to the letter, are made void, while those which are to be done after grace, with grace accompanying them, are upheld.

Let us see whether we can prove from the facts themselves that this is so. We read that the works of the law are destroyed when he crushes the pride of the Jews, saying: "Where is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law." Similarly he says to the Galatians: "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Christ Jesus, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law. For by the works of the law no flesh will be justified before him." And so impious error has said that works are made void, but with crafty cunning it has suppressed which works these were. Now, then, you will be spared the difficulty of understanding, if you grasp the distinction of persons and of works. For to the Jews it is said: "By the works of the law no flesh will be justified." But to Christians, already reborn in Christ, the word of instruction is directed thus: "Do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith"; and again: "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." To Christians, I say, it is said: "Let your light so shine before all men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven"; that is, not so that we may slacken into idleness, but so that we may boast of good works not in ourselves but in the Lord. To Christians it is said: "Truly I perceive that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him."
V. ON THE SAYING: "BY THE GRACE OF GOD I AM WHAT I AM."

Hear the apostle, in humble confession, mingling labour with grace: "But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not in vain, but I laboured more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me." See how to the gift of grace he always adds the service of labour. "Yet not I": because he had mentioned labour alone, he quickly ran back, as it were, to the embrace of grace, his mother, saying, "but the grace of God with me." "By the grace of God," he says, "I am." As one piously submissive, he ascribed the first part to grace alone; as a teacher of obedience, he assigned the middle to labour; and tempering both at the conclusion, he joined grace and labour together. He did not say, "I without grace," or "grace without me," but "the grace of God with me." How well he linked together at the end of his statement what he had first set out separately! And so, among the regenerate, when grace is mentioned in the Scriptures without labour, or labour without grace, the one is left unspoken, not separated. When one is spoken of without the other, the other is passed over in silence, not denied, according to the rule which Bishop Augustine teaches: "Not everything that is passed over in silence is denied."

And in another place the apostle says: "I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate." See: the blessed apostle, already won for Christ, already made a chosen vessel, by no means lets his hands go slack in idleness under the name of predestination and grace, but joins his own efforts to God's benefits and says: "I chastise my body and bring it into subjection." See, he is already a soldier on the right-hand side; and see how, though already proven, he fears danger; how, though chosen, he dreads being rejected. He already has victory in his hands, yet he does not lay down his arms; he has already been led to triumph, yet he still fears the outcome of the campaign. Since this is so, consider that you are rising up with the weapons of impious error not against some weak person but against the teaching of the greatest apostle, and contradicting Christ, who speaks within him. And while you take away the service of labour and the reasons for praying, recognize that you are shutting the door of salvation to the human race; and while you do not know how to flee the impiety of Pelagius, understand that you are turning aside to the pestilent doctrine of the Manichaeans, who deny free will entirely.

VI. HOW WE ARE TO UNDERSTAND: "BY GRACE YOU HAVE BEEN SAVED THROUGH FAITH, AND THIS NOT OF YOURSELVES, FOR IT IS THE GIFT OF GOD; NOT OF WORKS, LEST ANYONE SHOULD BOAST." HERE FAITH TOO IS COUNTED AMONG WORKS, AND THE FOOD OF THE LAW IS DESCRIBED AS PERISHING, WHILE THE FOOD OF GRACE ENDURES.

Just as, a friend of sloth and ignorant of distinctions, you have strayed from the path of understanding regarding the works of the law and the works of faith, so too, regarding the two times of grace, you have followed your own persuasion as the worst of guides and lost the shining rule of the catholic faith. The time of grace by which we were redeemed did not wait for human merits and did not seek works at all; God was content with the devotion of our faith alone, according to the apostle's words: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness"; as he also says in another place: "But my righteous one lives by faith. And if he draws back, my soul will take no pleasure in him." He declared him righteous and living by faith, because he remembers that he himself bestowed faith and righteousness on him when he sought them. But by saying, "if he draws back," he shows that when a man has turned aside of his own will into byways, he did not perish as one abandoned; he ungratefully withdrew himself from the mercy that was pressing itself upon him. Again, to the Hebrews: "Whoever draws near to God must believe that he exists and that he becomes the rewarder of those who seek him." How well he joined the part of the Lord and the part of the servant by saying, "he becomes the rewarder of those who seek him"! For as the bounty of rewarding belongs to God, so the devotion of seeking belongs to man.

But you say that faith itself cannot belong to everyone. It is no wonder that you strive to take faith away from man, since you deny that works pertain to him, for it is clear that faith is counted among works, as we have in the Gospel: "Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life." Here the food, that is, the understanding of the letter, is described as perishing, but the food of grace, that is, faith, as enduring. And so the passage continues: "The Jews said to him: What shall we do, that we may work the works of God? Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." Do you notice that nothing is done in the service of God without work, since even the one who believes is working? Again in the apostle: "Neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." Similarly also to the Thessalonians [the second letter]: "May God count you worthy of his calling and fulfil every good pleasure of goodness and the work of faith in you." And concerning Abraham, in the letter of the apostle James: "You see that faith was working together with his works, and by works faith was made complete." Recognize here a twofold duty, of working and of faith. "By grace," he says, "you have been saved through faith." So the first calling requires of us the short way of faith, but the grace of the following time lays on those who have been redeemed, washed and renewed the diligence of work and the care of laborious service, so that what we received without labour we may, with his help, keep with labour, as the apostle warns: "See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain." Recognize that the stages of calling and of completion are distinct. He expects faith from little ones; from those who have been strengthened he requires works as well as faith, yet in such a way that he increases the disposition of belief in those who make progress and stands by those who labour as their daily helper.
VII. AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT FREE WILL HAS BEEN ENTIRELY TAKEN AWAY.

The champion of this wicked persuasion thinks that man, enriched with understanding, endowed with reason, and adorned with the honour of the divine image, should be compared to brute animals and senseless beasts of burden, so that he is dragged onto the right way by no guidance of his own but only by the forceful command of his Maker. In this way he even strives to liken him to insensible elements. Lands produce nothing of their fruitfulness by their own choice; they are unaware of their own fertility; they have neither the freedom nor the will of any sense; yet harvests of crops are gathered from them by the work of a cultivator. So too, he holds, the fruits of righteousness and the desire for and progress in good things are to be gathered from man while he remains idle from every exercise of virtue, by God's action alone; and, as though he neither perceives nor consents to anything, whatever he desires or does is to be judged as in no way belonging to his own effort and endeavour. And as the great sea is rolled this way and that by the driving winds, so the human mind is turned to any good deed without any inclination of its own, by the sole impulse of divine power. If this is so, if understanding does not call man back from the left hand of evil, and if aspiration does not rouse him to the right hand of good, then he will no longer hold the condition of a man but of a beast.

See what kind of man the heretic, under the pretext of grace, wants man to be after grace! So if free will has entirely perished, which surely consists in the love of innocence, the working of righteousness, and the sanctification of the body, if this was entirely taken away in the first man's transgression, how is it that we read: "Learn righteousness, you who dwell on the earth"; and again: "But my righteous one lives by faith"; and: "The righteous shall possess the land as an inheritance"; and: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers"? Did innocence perish completely because its possessor neglected to stand firm in its first degree? I do not think so, for it is written: "The innocent and the upright have clung to me"; and again: "Who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent of hands and pure of heart"; and again: "The Lord will not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence." Must we believe that the sanctification of the body was entirely lost because the dignity of the original purity was shattered when the members of the rebellious servant failed to keep their own service? Certainly not, for we read: "That you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God"; and again: "Be holy, because I am holy." So, in this class of goods which the careless and overconfident dweller in paradise had received from his kindly Maker, the practice has not perished, even though the perfection has been lost. The chastity of these virtues, I say, has not perished, even though their virginal wholeness has been violated.
VIII. HOW THE WEAKNESS OF FREE WILL IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD.

But you ask and say: "How is the weakening of the human mind's free will to be understood?" Its freedom, having been diminished, requires the supports of grace all the more, just as a man worn out by long illness, with faltering step, has greater need of aids and comforts. Consider how, after an inveterate habit of self-indulgence, the restoration of self-control will cost much labour. Consider how sobriety, once held captive by long use of drunkenness, is scarcely recovered even with the violence of a harsh cross, though earlier, while it was kept unharmed, it was preserved with little effort, since an unviolated conscience is possessed with a certain pleasure. And consider how, after the various enticements of fleshly vices, which early youth, still keeping its own state, could easily have trampled underfoot, one returns to the way of virtue with great struggle, as though climbing a steep mountain. Just so, the freedom of human choice granted by God has lost the flower and vigour of its grace, yet it has not itself perished, so that it perceives the divine gifts not so much as forbidden to it, but as things it must seek again with the greatest labour and sweat, under the protection of his help.

Hear the lawgiver discussing the free choice of the will when he says: "I have set before your face life and death, good and evil. Choose life, that you may live"; and again: "I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgements." You see that here no necessity of fate or of imposed perdition presses upon anyone, where the power of choosing belongs to him; nor does predestination drag him to one side, where the choice of either side is offered to him. Again: "Let your hand be ready to save me, for I have chosen your commandments." That is to say: "The ruinous pleasure of the world tempted me toward the left side, but the profit of your commandments drew me to the right." So, since the Gentiles themselves are directed in their judgement of evil or good by the choice implanted in them, how much more can the humble Christian govern the freedom of his will toward the good side, since he places his ability in the power of God his helper, to whom it is said: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have"; and again: "Do you wish to be made well?" Knowing how much the mighty Maker has placed in the human heart, he asks for the will of the very man he is about to heal. And in another place he rebukes the people walking in the freedom of choice granted to them, thus: "Bring out the people who are blind yet have eyes, who are deaf yet have ears." Here it is understood that their being deaf and blind comes from obstinacy, not from nature. And in the Gospel he plainly shows that the disposition of good will has been placed in man: "If anyone wishes to come after me," he says, "let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." That is to say: "It is of my mercy that you are called, but it is entrusted to your will that you follow."

Let us see whether God invites man to himself through idleness. "Let him deny himself," he says; that is, let the one who is evil strive to be good and say in supplication: "And of my own will I will give thanks to him." Each person is commanded to turn of his own will, lest the sinner perhaps despair of being able to change for the better. "If anyone wishes to come after me," he says, "let him deny himself"; that is, let him become another man out of the one he was. Let patience overcome anger, let temperance curb desire, let humility drive out pride, let the cross crush pleasure. Who would suppose that these things are to be conferred on him while he sleeps, by grace alone, without labour of heart, without affliction of the flesh, without a great struggle of both the inner and the outer man? "Let him deny himself": that is to say, "O man, do not think that you were so made by your Maker that you cannot become righteous instead of wicked, chaste instead of self-indulgent, kind instead of malicious. For you to achieve this, it is not your making that must be changed, but your life." Now, in saying these things, we do not make labour equal to grace; rather, we set grace above it beyond all comparison.
IX. HOW WE ARE TO UNDERSTAND "IT DEPENDS NOT ON THE ONE WHO WILLS OR THE ONE WHO RUNS, BUT ON GOD WHO SHOWS MERCY," AND ALSO "I HAVE NOT COME TO CALL THE RIGHTEOUS, BUT SINNERS TO REPENTANCE."

But you say: so far is anything from belonging to man, and so wholly is everything God's grace, that the apostle says, "It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs." This is aimed at the Jew who claims it for himself on the basis of the law, or at Pelagius who presumes it on the strength of free choice. Even though human service has its part, the whole nevertheless depends on God who shows mercy, not on the one who wills or the one who runs. Here the apostle plainly singles out and rebukes the man who thinks he is sufficient for himself, without the hand of one who helps him. But to the man who joins his own efforts to the help of the merciful God he does not say, "not on the one who wills or the one who runs"; he speaks to him quite differently: "Run," he says, "so that you may win," and again: "You were running so well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?" If the will of the one who runs is not to be looked for as well, why is it said, "So I do not run aimlessly," and again, "I have finished the race, I have kept the faith"? "Not on the one who wills or the one who runs": a man wraps himself in the darkness of error if he does not know how to ask, in the holy Scriptures, about the persons and the circumstances. In this passage the apostle, in upholding the faith of the Gentiles, curbs and crushes the pride of the Jews, who claimed righteousness for themselves from the works of the law and spurned the mercy and grace of God; who, as the apostle says, "seeking to establish their own righteousness, did not submit to the righteousness of God."

In another place, too, he condemns them, granting them a pretended righteousness and speaking obliquely, with irony: "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." "The righteous" means those who flatter themselves with a presumed righteousness, just as elsewhere he rejects the Pharisee who justifies himself and accepts the tax collector who accuses himself. "I have not come," he says, "to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance"; that is, I have not come for the Jews, who claim the privileges of righteousness for themselves on the basis of the law, but rather I seek the Gentiles, who by faith profess repentance for their sins. With their arrogance in view he also says elsewhere: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." The Jews boasted that they were righteous and well, but they were not. Who, with a sound heart, would dare to call himself well, when the whole human race lay sick, struck by a single bite of the serpent? So the sick man has one hope of health: to acknowledge himself sick before the physician. And the man who pretends not to know his illness deserves to go without the remedy. That is why there will be more joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance. Who would not believe, from this passage, that those who need no repentance are truly righteous? Yet no one needs salvation more than the man who does not see that he needs it. And so the true shepherd rejoices more over one sheep called back from straying than over ninety-nine sheep that did not stray. And who could be free from the evil of deadly straying, when the prophet testifies, "All we like sheep have gone astray; each has turned aside to his own way"? How lamentable was the blindness of the Jews, which, by denying the Savior, had lost the way and refused to recognize its own straying!

So in this passage the divine word, under the name of "the righteous," while not ruling out another sense, chiefly marks and rebukes the arrogance of the Jews. For while the number ten and the number one hundred signify the righteous and the perfect, nine and ninety-nine, by the very nature of an imperfect number, signify the unrighteous and sinners. In this passage, then, the apostle's teaching chastises the pride of the Jew, who justified himself by the law and rejected the mercy of the Redeemer, by saying "not on the one who wills": for in the humble Christian obedience and submission are themselves a running and an ascent, while in the pride of the Jew they are a fall and a running down. "Not," he says, "on the one who wills or the one who runs." How can that saying apply to the faithful man who is subject to Christ's laws, of whom it is said, "and his will was in the law of the Lord"; and, as we said before, "If anyone wills to come after me"; and, "I will sacrifice to you willingly, O Lord"; and, "Whoever wills to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it"? See how great and how arduous a work, the losing and finding of one's life, he has placed in the will of man as well, and how he therefore concluded: "For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each according to his works." Notice that when he says "according to his works," the giver of grace has placed man's salvation not in the predestination of the Maker but in the working of the servant. So what is meant here is not man's condition but his conduct, and that is why he says elsewhere: "We shall all stand before the judgment seat of God, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil." Recognize that in this passage it is not the evils of another, of one's race or origin, but one's own deeds in the body that are to be examined at the last judgment.

Therefore it is clear that in a man reborn in Christ what is to be called to account is not what he was born with but what he has done. If, then, a man's action does not also belong to his will, how can he say, "If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land"? God, the maker of both the outer and the inner man, arranged the members of the human body by his power, and by his ordinance he allowed man to direct and manage the service and use of those members. And just as he himself formed the right hand in every man, yet placed it in man's power to stretch it out wherever he wished and to apply it to various tasks, so in the same way he implanted, breathed and poured into every soul the faculty of reason and the choice of the will, yet left that will in the hand of human counsel to be governed and exercised, and entrusted its functions to man's right and dominion. Thus, if in his depravity he sought evil, he would know that it was allowed him in the freedom of his choice, but would not know it to be lawful; and if he desired good, he would ask his Maker for the doing and completing of it, while dutiful devotion would earn its reward. And so the one who formed and rules man assigned to man the use of a good will and reserved its effect for himself. He did not, then, grant willing to one and deny it to another, which would be neither fair nor just; but just as he gave every man a hand, an eye and the ability to walk, so likewise he granted every man a will, to turn in whatever direction he chose. Righteousness in man, then, is not a personal gift of God but a general and public one. The way to lay hold of salvation is like a spring set in the middle of this world and given to all in common, open for everyone to draw from, so that whoever neglects to draw from it is rightly answerable to the giver.

So what is to be demanded back from all has been offered to all. For if, as they say, there is a special dispensation regarding man's salvation, I do not see how there can be a general examination. But since he says, "We must all appear before the judgment seat of God," he would not demand it terrifyingly from all unless he had mercifully offered it to all. Accordingly, the apostle exhorts the man set in readiness for battle in these words: "Toil like a good soldier of Christ. No one serving God as a soldier entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who approved him. For one who competes in a contest is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules." And again: "The farmer who toils ought to be the first to receive a share of the crops." Listen to the apostle elsewhere too, not preaching your idleness: "Finally, brothers," he says, "be strong in the Lord and in the might of his power. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the world rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having been perfected in all things, to stand. Stand, then, with your loins girded in love, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace, taking up in all things the shield of faith, with which you can quench all the flaming arrows of the most wicked one." When he says "so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil," and again "so that you may be able to resist on the evil day," and then "taking up the shield of faith, with which you can quench all the flaming arrows of the most wicked one," he shows most clearly that God has granted every man the capacity of choice, by which he is ready not only to resist his own flesh but also to fight against the devil, of whom he says elsewhere: "Be watchful," he says, "because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour."

If, as you claim, a necessity laid on them by their origin had already assigned certain people to this adversary, he would not be looking for people to deceive, and watchfulness would do no good to those already assigned. But it is not so. For just as the enemy advances against all, so the right hand of protection and help is denied to none, and those who pray and keep watch are succored by the kindness of mercy, which is surely granted to those who knock more because of their devotion than because of predestination. Amid all this, does it not seem to you that the man who says grace alone suffices, without the exercise of work and toil, bursts out with a deranged mind into this blasphemous cry: Let no one keep vigil, no one fast, no one punish the assault of lust by the contrition of abstinence; let no one declare war on vices by mortifying the outer man, no one strive against the wounds of the inner man's anxiety [?] by salutary affliction; let no one resist lust, no one seek remedies for his crimes through the toil of a wasted body; let no one beat back with the power of the cross the enemy armed with the enticements of obscene pleasure, but let him bare his chest to the enemy's flaming arrows; let no one redeem with the sacrifices of almsgiving the debts that make him liable to eternal death, no one tend his wounds through works of mercy and righteousness, but let him carry them untouched to the day of judgment? See: the man who a little while ago was thought a champion of grace is found, by blocking the way of human salvation, to be an assailant of the grace through which salvation itself has been bestowed, and is shown to have gone over to the devil's counsels as an accomplice in perdition.
X. AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT MAN HAS FREE CHOICE READY ONLY FOR EVIL, AND NONE AT ALL FOR GOOD.

Where, then, is the prophet's saying, "Listen to me, you who pursue what is right and seek the Lord," or the apostle's: "Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves to obey him, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness"? When the apostle demands better pursuits of man, he shows that man has the capacity for a good will; and when we put this forward, we openly proclaim the ordinance and wonderful arrangement of man's Maker. The same apostle shows that this capacity was prepared for righteous duties when he says: "Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Do not present your members to sin as weapons of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members to God as weapons of righteousness." Likewise: "I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to wickedness, leading to wickedness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to sanctification." Is he not here urging to the pursuit of good works the very same man whom he shows to have been given over to evil before?

So when the destroyer of free choice declares that everything, in one direction or the other, has been settled and fixed by predestination, he also, in a spirit of headlong impiety, makes void the last remedies of repentance. And how can he preach grace who denies mercy? How can he seem to uphold the gift of God when he takes away his help? How does he dare to presume to cite testimonies from the Scriptures when he tries to shut out the benefits of the Scriptures? How can I be told, "Turn away from evil and do good," if I am already unable to turn away from evil? Why does the apostle say, "Put to death your members," and again, "You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light"? How can the preacher of the law urge me to change, if the Maker has laid on me an unchangeable law: "stripping off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new"? How can you contend that the ingrained stain of sin belongs inseparably to our origin and condition, when you know that it can be laid aside and stripped off? Understand that you are speaking by a contrary spirit against the Holy Spirit, who gave the world the mysteries of the law and the prophets and the oracles of gospel truth for its help, and who promised the kingdom of heaven to those who keep the divine commandments through the duties of laborious service, with grace working alongside them.

Therefore measure the honor of holy work and toil by the greatness and dignity of its reward; for you undoubtedly judge its palm and crown cheap if you maintain that it can be won without toilsome contrition. Can the command of the divine precept be fulfilled without great effort and work: "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good," or this: "Do not be deceived: bad company corrupts good morals"? And how, amid these, can you assert that the gift of grace once received is in no danger, when you read that the good implanted in our character can be corrupted by evil? Will it be by idleness that one attains what the apostle says: "In all things we suffer affliction, but are not crushed; we are perplexed, but not left destitute; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but we do not perish"; and what he says elsewhere: "The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world"? If these things and others like them, of which the holy Scriptures are full, are gained through idleness, why are they not gained by everyone? Much will be taken away both from the glory of the one rewarded and from the justice of the one who rewards, if the highest and most illustrious men are crowned for rest and sloth. And where is that saying of the prophet: "Because of the words of your lips I have kept to hard ways"? If the business of seeking salvation is an idle affair, the way of virtue is common, general and broad; then the Gospels lie when they say, "How narrow is the gate and hard the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!" If works cease, merits will have no honor; if there is nothing arduous in toil, there will be nothing precious in virtue.

But this arduous way offends the lazy, and toil deters the idle. The cause, then, is not the coercion of the one who foreknows but the disobedience of the one who sins, as we read: "They perished because of their iniquities, like the dream of one who wakes"; and again: "Depart from me, all you who work iniquity"; and elsewhere: "They did not keep God's covenant, and they refused to walk in his law." It is not impossibility, then, that draws a man away from the work of righteousness, but iniquity and his own will. And since the apostle says, "Rebuke the one who sins in the presence of all," there would be no reason to rebuke or condemn someone who does wrong against his will. But it is not so. For since the Lord says through his prophet, "I will judge each one according to his ways, O house of Israel," whoever has yielded to passion was not overcome under the pressure of foreknowledge but was led astray by the allurement of sin. Those who still deny the effort of human toil set against us this testimony: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain." Those who raise this objection unskillfully and believe that everything must be denied to man cannot even make their reading work by the plain sound of the words. For does the Lord administer the salvation of the human race by himself alone, as a solitary steward? Certainly not. But just as the body, arranged in its members, carries out the command of the head, so the Lord builds his house through the leaders and shepherds of the Church, through those who say, "For we are God's fellow workers." For whoever takes up the care of saving a man is a helper of the Redeemer.

So the Lord builds this house through his saints, and the saints build it through their Lord. The Church is built by the one who said, "Like a wise master builder I laid the foundation." Do you know of the Church being built in any other way than through the labors and duties of priests, the ministries and examples of the saints, the mighty deeds of the apostles and the deaths of the martyrs? Yet amid all this, although the servant must labor even to the point of enduring every evil and losing his life, the effect of the labor must always be ascribed to the Lord. But to anyone who presumes to claim for himself either the beginning of the work or its end, it is rightly said: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain." Moreover, just as the devotion of tireless service is to be expected from man, so the completion of the finished work is to be credited to the Lord, whose gifts are lacking only to the one who neglected to keep them. For that servant too knew that he had received, who scorned to double the talent entrusted to him by the business of salvation and instead committed it to the earth in sluggish idleness. Saul, too, received the grace of God when he was anointed by Samuel, and obtained special favor and royal power on this condition: that he should not turn aside from God's commandments. And he who, with the priest as his teacher, had overthrown the groves and shrines along with their mediums, lost his faith when his teacher died, and later flew to the deceitful answers of a woman medium, though by overthrowing the idols he had shown that he could have belonged to God.
XI. AGAINST THE VIEW OF THOSE WHO SAY THAT A VESSEL FOR DISHONOR CANNOT RISE [?] TO BECOME A VESSEL FOR HONOR.

They say that a vessel of dishonour cannot pass into a vessel of honour, because the apostle said: “Does not the potter have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” In this passage, by his concise way of speaking, he left unstated the prior causes by which a person passes into either honour or dishonour. For when a person has begun through grace to be a vessel of honour, he must keep watch so that the honour he has received is preserved with God’s cooperation. Otherwise the man who has been won may later be turned into a vessel of dishonour when guilt arises. They also say that a man’s worse state, fixed beforehand from the beginning of his life, cannot be changed for the better. That is believed to be what will happen there, after we depart this life, in the underworld, where there will no longer be any amendment or change. Until then, right up to the end, the very worst can pass over to righteousness, and the perfect have reason to fear danger. As we read in 1 Samuel: “Those who glorify me I will glorify, but those who despise me shall be held in no honour.” Why is this one honoured and that one despised? Surely for this reason: the one who brought dishonour could also have glorified God, and the one who gave glory could also have despised him. The one who chose to please the Lord his God could also have chosen not to, and the one who chose not to could have chosen to. And do not think that there is a difference of nature here. The one who wills and the one who does not will are the same.

Therefore no one reborn in Christ can be a vessel of offence and wrath unless he has first become a vessel of malice through his own fault. Conversely, to become a vessel of mercy he must first be a vessel of obedience, so that the sentence of the just judge follows upon causes that came before it. Let us show that a vessel of dishonour can pass into a vessel of honour by God’s help and its own effort: “If,” he says, “I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and does justice and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die.” What is the wicked man but a vessel of dishonour? See how through the remedy of repentance he is suddenly honoured with the brightness of grace and clothed with the beauty of righteousness. With the dregs of his sins wiped away, he can say confidently with the prophet: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be clean; you will wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow.” Hear the apostle declare that the stains of conscience can be washed white, so that a vessel of iniquity may become a vessel of sanctification: “In a great house,” he says, “there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honour and some for dishonour.” O human race, lift up a heart set free from unchangeable necessity, and recognise your Lord’s inexpressible goodness toward the salvation of mankind. After saying “some for honour and some for dishonour,” he opened and held out a hand of hope to the faithful, saying: “If anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified.”

The vessel of the heart, then, can hold either thing. What it once allowed to be poured into it can easily be emptied out by a change of its former purpose, so that the very same vessel remains once the iniquity within it has been poured out. So the vessel belongs to man’s substance, while what is stored in the vessel belongs to the kind and variety of the will. In another place the Lord shows that what was lost can be restored, when he says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and again: “It was right to feast and rejoice, because this son of mine was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and has been found.” So the loss had not taken place in his nature. He who had died through the contempt that made him leave came back to life through his desire to return. For just as it was his own crime that he fled far from the eyes of his loving father, so it was his own devotion that he took thought by the good implanted in him, rose up, and ran back to his father’s embrace. But the grace that had knocked at the door of the wanderer was the same grace that welcomed him on his return. Away, then, with any determination by origin or by fate! See: the dead man is brought to life and the lost is found. So too the woman in the Gospel who had lost a drachma in the house (that is, the possession of some gift or of salvation) searched for it with a lit lamp. She brought her own effort to the oil of grace, and the seeker’s purpose joined itself to God’s help, and so what she had lost within, she found within.

If, then, a person at any time strives by the judgement of his mind to become bad from good or good from bad, it is the will, which is free and given by God, that is being redirected; it is not the force of predestination at work. You read in the sacred pages: “On whatever day you turn and groan, then you will be saved,” and again: “I do not desire the death of the wicked man, but that the wicked man turn from his way and live. Turn from your most wicked ways,” and again: “The wickedness of the wicked man shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his injustice,” and also: “Cast out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump.” Each time a person rejects what is worse and turns to better things with the help of grace, he is made from a vessel of dishonour into a vessel of honour. But human frailty more readily admits that the good should become bad, passing from a vessel of honour into a vessel of dishonour. So we read in Habakkuk: “and his food is choice,” of which it is also said: “He will count gold as straw.” Jeremiah, too, says: “How the gold has grown dim, how the finest colour has changed!” The apostle likewise says: “Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot?”

The meaning is plain, then: through his own fault a person can be changed from being part of the body of Christ into the devil’s portion. Elsewhere he teaches in the most absolute terms that the best can become the worst and that God’s temple can be violated, saying: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him.” See: it is already known to be God’s temple and already possessed by the Holy Spirit, and yet we are told that through carelessness it can be violated, corrupted, and taken over by an unworthy guest. In the same way the prophet rebukes the soul that has willingly emptied itself of God’s grace: “I planted a choice vine, wholly true. How have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” See: he shows that a vine planted by God from a noble root, and chosen by the care of its cultivator, has been spoiled by its own crime. That is why he says of it in the song of Isaiah: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” The expectation of the farmer who rebukes it shows that this vine could have yielded the fruits of righteousness. He testifies that one who stands can fall, saying: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.” Conversely, he says to one who lies fallen: “Shall not he who falls rise again? For God is able to make him stand.” In this way he openly shows that a person’s state can be turned in different directions, not by God’s decree but by the freedom of choice. Isaiah, too, clearly affirms that what is corrupted can be set right and what is stained can be washed clean, when he says to sinners: “Wash yourselves, be clean, remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes.”
XII. Likewise it is plain that willing and not willing were entrusted to human choice, toward the good as well as toward the bad.

Meanwhile we must carefully ask the heretics whether man cannot do good, or will not. Scripture clearly assigns to man implanted seeds of good will when it says: “If you will keep the commandments, they will preserve you,” and: “Do not fall away from the discipline of the Lord,” and: “Do not refrain from doing good to the needy,” and: “Do not devise evil against your friend,” and: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding,” and: “Do not reject your mother’s counsel,” and: “Do not heed a deceitful woman,” and: “He would not understand, so as to do good,” and: “They would not accept discipline.” When someone is reproached for not willing, this clearly shows that willing was within his reach. There are many similar passages in the words of the Old Testament, and all of them specifically bind and convict the will itself. In the new books of the Gospels and the apostles, too, what else is shown but freedom of the will, where it is said: “Do not store up treasures on earth,” and: “Do not fear those who kill the body”? “Be sober and righteous, and do not sin.” To Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you.” “And let your good deed not be done as if from necessity, but from free will.” He even admonishes slaves to serve their masters from the heart with good will. Elsewhere: “Do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality.” “Do not speak against one another,” and: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap,” and: “Do not love the world or the things in the world.”

We see, then, that the consent of the human mind can pass both to the good side and to its opposite. That is why he says elsewhere: “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap if we do not grow weary. So let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith.” “Do not love the world,” he says. Had he not given man an inclination toward better things, he would not forbid him the appetite for evil. So the one whom his Lord calls to the right is dragged to the left by his own crime. Therefore he says again: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” Clearly, one who is promised victory for choosing the good is not pressed into evil by necessity. No law of origin drags off the road a man whom his Maker has set at a fork in it. So if someone who was given a will able to overcome evil happens to yield to his adversary, what he lacked was the courage to fight, not the chance of winning. We read in Hebrews: “For if we sin willfully after receiving knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” On this basis, if we do not have freedom of choice, how do we sin willfully? If you ask why such a man is guilty, it is because after receiving knowledge of the truth he turned aside to the spirit of error. “After receiving knowledge,” it says: understand that he had received grace and lost it through negligence. And again: “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and regarded as defiled the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

Why is he accused on the testimony of two or three witnesses and put to death as guilty of his own crime, if he is already weighed down by an inescapable law of nature that makes him sin? Without doubt he deserves punishment because he could have kept righteousness and would not. If you ask why he was stripped of so great a good, it is because, as it says, he insulted the Spirit of grace. Notice in this passage that grace did not fail man by being denied to him. Rather, man first abandoned and despised the kindness of the giver, and only then did it abandon him. He rebukes with a kind of grief the insult of the one who spurns it. So when such a man willingly turned off the road, he did not perish as one abandoned. He ungratefully withdrew himself from the mercy that offered itself to him, and became like those of whom the psalmist declares: “And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly.” In what follows he gives the reasons the blessing was lost: “And their own vanities,” he says, “led them astray, and led them astray in a trackless place and not on the way.” Here the transgressor of the commandment was shown to be guilty precisely because he was seduced into evil rather than forced into it. Likewise, writing to the Galatians, he lays the guilt of the transgression at the door of man’s own offence, saying: “Formerly, when you did not know God, you served beings that by nature are not gods.” It follows from this that Christ, whom we are commanded to serve, is God by nature. It continues: “But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how is it that you turn back to the weak and beggarly elements, which you wish to serve all over again?” He did not say, “You cannot be good,” but, “You wish to be bad.” Had they been unable to stand firm in the good once corrected, they would not be rebuked for slipping back into worse. To them he says again: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you.”

See: these people, begotten by faith, had become like miscarriages, yet he asserts that they can still be re-formed into the image of Christ. By still calling his lost children sons, he condemns their transgression without despairing of them. He teaches that what is lost can be restored and that what has been given can be taken away. Elsewhere the heretic interprets the apostle’s statement as referring to God’s predestination or predetermination, where we read: “I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will show mercy to whom I have mercy.” He must be asked whether what God wills is ordered or disordered, just or unjust. When he answers that it must be just, he must be told: “Take these, then, to be words of justice, for the divine will is justice.” So the statement “I will have mercy on whom I will” is to be understood as follows: on the one whose purpose I recognise as just, whose ready faith I see, whom I observe obeying my commands, whom I find doing my will. “And I will show mercy,” he says, “to whom I have mercy.” This should be understood as follows: whoever keeps the mercy bestowed by God with a submissive and careful mind will obtain greater mercy. As he says elsewhere: “For to him who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance.” That is, whoever guards God’s gift once received with vigilance and fear of heart will receive ever greater increase of that grace, so that his very progress gives birth to further progress. As it says elsewhere: “And let the holy still be sanctified.”

They also think that the apostle’s words should be referred to God’s predetermination: “So then he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills. You will say to me then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?’” Clearly, the apostle here introduces a contrary view, put in the mouth of a questioner or objector. He chastises this view from the opposing side with the rebuke that follows: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does not the potter have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” Here he curbs the curiosity of the unbeliever with the authority of one who rebukes.
