When he says, “Does not he have power,” he sets God’s power alone against the slanderer and does not stoop to give him the reason for it, since this man ignorantly and faithlessly ascribed all human acts to divine decree. “Does not the potter have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” In saying “from the same lump,” he addresses whoever supposed that there are two lumps of the human race: learn from sacred Scripture that there is one. What makes two is the perversity of men’s pursuits and the diversity of their wills. So each person becomes a vessel of dishonour or of honour according to the character of these, not by God’s impulse.
XIII. In which it is shown from the testimonies of Scripture that the grace of God and human will are joined together.

If you pay close attention, you will see clearly and abundantly how the pages of holy Scripture assert now the power of grace and now the assent of the human will. We show the frailty of our choice when we say to God: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door to enclose my lips.” Again, the divine word gives a command, showing that the strength of choice can do something, when it says to man: “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit.” The word of wisdom commends choice when it says: “Keep your heart with all vigilance.” But the apostle shows that this cannot be done without divine help when he says: “May the Lord guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.” The prophet asserts the capacity of his own will, saying of himself: “I have inclined my heart to perform your statutes.” But he understands that nothing should be presumed from his own strength alone when he cries out to God: “Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to covetousness.” Because of free choice we are commanded: “Make straight paths for your feet and direct your ways.” But conscious of our weakness, we take refuge in grace and pray: “Direct my way in your sight,” and: “Perfect my steps in your paths.”

He who by his general dispensation has granted us the right of our own will commands us: “Light for yourselves the light of knowledge.” But because everything must be referred to the author of grace, we read: “He who teaches man knowledge,” or: “The Lord gives light to the blind,” and again: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death,” and: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law.” The apostle, the preacher of free choice, spurs its freedom on by saying: “Guard your souls.” But he bears witness to God’s mercy when he says: “The Lord guard your going in and your coming out.” These passages sometimes assert the freedom of choice and sometimes show the bounty of heaven. In some, man is reminded of the powers he has been granted, so that he does not sit idle hoping in grace alone. In others, he is commanded to hope in grace, so that he does not feel secure in his own labour alone. But you say: “If there is no predestination, why are some infants baptised while others are snatched away without the sanctification of baptism?” It is the trick of a serpent to leave the light and flee into dark caverns, when throughout all its volumes sacred Scripture clearly speaks of free choice. What sense is there in wanting to ask about hidden things, when you see that the things made plain answer your concern most fully? What use is it to leave aside what is certain and inquire into what is uncertain, about which you find nothing written in catholic Scripture? Do you not understand that you wrong the truth by probing whatever the truth did not want you to know? You propose to discuss the nature of free choice, and then by a pernicious error you slip into discussing the condition of infancy, in which no trace at all of free choice, and no sign of a will of one’s own, can appear.
XIV. Against their claim that those who perish after baptism never truly believed in baptism.

Here we must reply by asking: in what author do you read this, and on what teacher’s authority do you presume to assert it? You do not deny that original sin is abolished in baptism, and baptism is proven valid wherever the undivided Trinity is invoked. Then give the reasons why someone who has been baptised still remains under the debt of original sin. “They too,” you say, “perish in Adam, because they did not believe in baptism.” Were you not saying a little earlier that human effort is not required in order to obtain God’s gifts? See, you yourself most plainly profess that the generosity of the giver is void without the devotion of the recipient. You yourself, I say, confirm that without the merit of faith (that is, without the cooperation of the human will) grace is of no use. And yet you say that God has reserved to himself everything concerning man’s state and given nothing to man.

See, even by your own account the mystery of regeneration cannot stand firm unless a person brings a disposition of belief to match the gift of blessing. Why do you demand assent from one to whom you deny effort? Now the prophet says: “Living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem,” by which he signifies the sacraments of the life-giving water. How, then, can the renewed man still keep with him the bond of the old man, which has been cancelled? How can one who has been absolved in Christ rise again still carrying the debt of Adam? How can the life that flows from the sacred font still bring forth death along with God’s adopted son? For the apostle says: “All of you who were baptised into Christ have put on Christ.” No one at all can put him on without first putting off the garments of his first birth. And who came to baptism of his own will, yet can be shown by you to have gained nothing from it? Even a heretic regenerated in the name of the Trinity receives so much from the very power of the mystery that, if he later passes over to the faith of Christ, he does not need to be baptised again. He is judged to have been washed by the working of grace, so that he need only be clothed with the blessing of chrism. The catholic Church detests this reprobate notion that you hold. “That is why,” you say, “those who have been immersed in the water of birth still do not receive the gift of baptism: they come to baptism without faith.” It is not so. Notice that the very act of coming to baptism and desiring salvation already belongs to faith. “Whoever perishes after baptism,” you say, “perishes in Adam, because they did not believe in baptism.” You would be more correct to say that such people perished after baptism because they would not join the duty of labour to the gift of grace. Negligent habit and sloth of heart drew them away from vigilance in good works and from diligence in careful service.

But if the fault of unbelief is the cause of perdition, what shall we think of infants? Through the devotion of their parents and the simplicity of nursing infancy, the full vigilance of faith is credited to them. Without any danger of unbelief they obtain the spotless gifts of regeneration, and yet many of them, as they grow older, plunge headlong into death. What reason accounts for this, except that, as sloth weakens them, they [?]…
XV. On the fall of the angel, and that the holy angels bear the likeness of God, against the persuasion of certain people.

[?] … and he explained why they were seen to be broken off: "Because of unbelief," he says, "they were broken off" — not, certainly, because of foreknowledge. He teaches that God's generosity is not confined to believers, since he shows that even those he charges with unbelief could have believed. In this way he also makes clear that even unbelievers received the means of faith. And while he says that the natural branches were broken off, he checked the presumptuous with a saving rebuke: "If," he says, "he did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either." And he added: "And they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. God is able to graft them in again." So here he speaks to both largeness of heart and humility of heart: to humility, so that even the one who has been grafted in may fear being broken off; to largeness of heart, so that even the one who has been broken off may not give up hope of reward. So the diligent shepherd searched for the lost sheep, and when he had found it he put it on his shoulders and carried it back to the fold. How could he abandon one who follows him, when he follows even one who abandons him?
16. AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT CHRIST DID NOT DIE FOR ALL.

They say that our Lord Jesus Christ did not take human flesh for the salvation of all, and did not die for all. The catholic Church utterly abhors this. For if it were so, how could the apostle say: "As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive"? Here one cannot say that "all" stands for a part. For just as the first part of the sentence plainly shows that all die in Adam, so without doubt the words that follow, "in Christ all will be made alive," are meant by the apostle to apply to all being made alive in Christ, not in part but universally. That is, even the ungodly are believed to be raised by the power of Christ's resurrection, although they rise not to be judged but to be punished. And when the apostle says, "who is the Savior of all people, especially of believers," in saying "of all people" he had in view the purpose of God's goodness; in saying "especially of believers" he singled out and distinguished in this place those who received the Redeemer's gifts through faith, through obedience, through a submissive will.

The same apostle declares that Christ came for all: "The love of Christ urges us on," he says, "because we have concluded this: if one died for all, then all have died. And he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them." Since, then, the general resurrection belongs to the power of redemption, if redemption does not extend to all, neither will resurrection extend to all. And so, just as we shall all rise, though we shall not all be changed, so we bear witness that the Lord our Redeemer came bringing the gift of a universal mercy, even though unbelief did not receive it, because it did not want to. For whoever at any time sought God found him, and whoever seemed not to have found him did not seek him. But if, as reckless ungodliness blasphemes, some are seen to be foreordained to death and others predestined to life, then Christ had no reason to come and no need to die, such as his love found.

A new remedy, then, could have achieved nothing if an ancient decree had settled human affairs before the ages. But because the fatalistic belief that brings in the force of a compelling foreknowledge must be utterly rejected, God all the more gave the law and raised up prophets in the intervening times, because he knew that the free choice of the human will had been weakened, not taken away. For if its strength had perished entirely, how could we read: "And his will was in the law of the Lord," and again: "Willingly will I sacrifice to you, O Lord," and in the letter to Philemon: "so that your goodness might not be by compulsion but voluntary"? And since he says in the Gospel, "It is my flesh that I will give for the life of the world," we must not doubt at all that he spent himself for the whole world, he who gave more than the whole world was worth, as the blessed evangelist John also testifies: "For he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and also for those of the whole world."

But you say: How did he redeem the whole world? Look, we see people living in their sins; how shall we think those redeemed whom we see remaining captive? Here let us gain understanding from a comparison. Suppose, for example, that an envoy or a priest, intending to intercede for a captive city, brings a generous ransom and receives the whole captive population from the hand of the one who held them by right of war, and every law and constraint of servitude is completely loosed. And suppose that meanwhile the pleasure of habit or some smooth-talking brigand entices certain of the captives there, and each of them, a slave to his own will, refuses the free gift. Has the contempt of the ungrateful lessened the grace of the ransom? Has the one who rejected freedom diminished in any way the kindness of the redeemer? Not at all. On the contrary, just as the one who returned can be pleasing to the redeemer, so the one who stayed behind is guilty of contempt. For he who rewards wills redeemed the willing. God, the just judge, desires that the one he remembers fell not unwillingly should return willingly. This being so, tell me whom he excluded from the grace of redemption, he who blotted out the bond of the ancient condemnation that stood against all.
AGAINST THEIR INTERPRETING A SAYING OF THE GOSPEL IN AN IGNORANT AND PERVERSE SENSE.

"No one," he says, "comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." Who could be so forgetful of his own salvation as to dare deny the mercy of the one who draws? But the truly ungodly man is he who declares that this mercy is not pressed upon all and not bestowed on all. In this passage he thinks that the salvation of the one drawn is an act of force by the one who draws. It is clear that one who does not know the bonds of devoted love knows only the chains of servile bondage. This divine saying, however, is aimed specifically at the man who claims everything for his own powers and presumes impiously on his own effort. Since, between the two sides, one judges that everything must be credited to effort and the other that everything must be credited to grace, the Greek saying is fulfilled in both: "Excesses," it says, "are inequalities." It is shown to be the same perversity and an equal impiety whether everything is ascribed to grace alone or everything to effort alone. What, then, should we hold between these, except always to subordinate effort to grace and always to join grace with effort?

But above all let us shun arrogance about our effort and claim nothing for ourselves on account of its merits, lest we be seen to imitate the Pharisee in the deadly presumption of boasting. For when he prayed, he certainly spoke the truth — "I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess" — yet he emptied the truth of its credit, because he mixed vanity with truth. So it is not doing good works but pride of heart that must be avoided. "No one," he says, "comes to me unless the Father draws him." Is a man to be moved and dragged from place to place like senseless, inert matter? No: as the Lord stands by and calls, the servant stretches out the hand of faith by which he may be drawn, and says: "I believe, Lord; help my unbelief." And so these two come together, the power of the one who draws and the willingness of the one who obeys, as when a sick man tries to get up, and his strength does not follow his intention, and so he begs for a hand to be held out to him. The will cries out, because weakness cannot lift itself up on its own. So the Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises up the striving. And what is drawing, if not preaching, rousing by the consolations of the Scriptures, deterring by rebukes, setting forth what is to be desired, holding out what is to be feared, threatening judgment, promising reward?

Hear the Lord drawing not with harsh chains but with the hands of hope, and inviting with the arms of love, as the prophet says: "I drew them with the bonds of love," and again: "We will run after you toward the fragrance of your ointments." And so he says: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you," so that no one who is shown to have been invited can excuse himself as having been shut out. For although he foreknew that not all would obey, he had nevertheless given to all both to will and to be able. Here we must ask more carefully whether each person wants to be drawn or not. If he does not want to, he simply does not deserve the kindness of the one who draws. But if he does want to, then already human consent is working together with God. "No one," he says, "comes to me unless the Father draws him." Since you see the one who draws, why do you pretend not to see the one who comes? And so, just as being drawn belongs to grace, so following is shown to belong to obedience. If this mercy of God who draws is given to the worthy, you notice that it is already bestowed, in some measure, upon the zeal of human service; but if it is given to the unworthy, it follows that it is not denied even to the reprobate, and that by evident compassion God's goodness is offered without distinction to the righteous and to sinners alike.

But the one you see drawing requires, by all means, someone who keeps the commandments, so that the one who is called may be grasped and drawn by a kind of handle of the will. If you think that he draws the unwilling, you lay the burden of injustice on heavenly justice. But if he is found to draw even the unwilling, how much more does he embrace those who desire him! For even the one who seems to be drawn without effort will have to labor in order to cling to the one who draws him. How many came and went away, because, though they had been drawn, they refused to persevere in grace even as he who longed for them was calling! As it is written in the Gospel: "Many of his disciples, when they heard this, went back and no longer walked with him"; and again: "Jesus said to the Twelve, 'Do you also want to go away?' Peter answered him, 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of God.'" In both cases the will was free: in the former, to depart with an ungrateful mind; in the latter, to remain in the freedom of faith.
17. AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT GOD BY FORCE HARDENS A MAN SO THAT HE CANNOT COME TO SALVATION.

If he himself hardens, as you blasphemously say, how does he say in the psalm: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," and again: "By your hardness and your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath," and likewise in Jeremiah: "You struck them, and they felt no pain; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction. They made their faces harder than rock, and they refused to return"? Notice further the cause of hardening, according to the saying of the most wise Solomon: "When the ungodly man has come into the depths of evil, he becomes contemptuous" — that is, from constant sinning despair is born, and from despair hardening is produced. When Jeremiah says, "They refused to return," you see that hardness of heart is the fault of one's own will. The shameless, greedy and bloodthirsty man is the slave of any crime whatever, if he does not struggle against his sins.

Let us see, then, where this hardening comes from. The occasion of hardening is certainly not the force of one who compels, but the clemency of one who forgives; and while untiring goodness bears with the offender in the hope of repentance, proud complacency abuses the kindness of the one who forgives. That is why the blessed apostle says: "Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and forbearance, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God's righteous judgment." You notice that by saying "by your hardness and impenitent heart" the apostle ascribes the fault of the hardened heart not to God but to man: "not knowing," he says, "that God's kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God's righteous judgment." Recognize that it is not God's severity but his goodness that hardens the hearts of the wicked. For because, through God's patience, they are not afflicted by the hardships and scourges of tribulation, they are corrupted by pride. The prophet too plainly records that this is so, saying: "They are not in the troubles of men, nor will they be scourged like other men; therefore their pride has taken hold of them." And so, while punishment is held back for the judgment and while the Lord's forbearance calls them to amendment, impunity nourishes contempt in the servant. "Who renders," he says, "to each according to his works." Surely God does not, by his foreknowledge, impose on man a necessity of sinning, when we read that he will demand an account from each according to his works. "I sinned," says the prophet, "and what sorrow befell me?" That is to say: it is certain that God does not know about sins, since he does not hasten punishment in vengeance. And again: "For he said in his heart: God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, so as never to see." So when he says "God has forgotten," he takes the patience of one who forgives for the negligence of one who does not know, and thinks forgotten what the magnanimous steward is keeping for later. In this way the warning of God's chastisement corrects the one who fears, while the gentleness of God's restraint hardens the scornful all the more, so that the ungodly man thinks that God, darkened by ignorance, never sees whatever his forbearing kindness for the present declines to punish. And though the contempt is clearly the insulter's own, God is thought to have caused the hardening. For in holding back his wrath while sins multiply, he allows the sinner to insult him.
18. AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT PEOPLE ARE DRIVEN TO DEATH BY THE WILL OF GOD.

But if, as the heretic says, people are dragged to perdition by the will of God, how is it that in the reading from Kings the woman says to David: "God does not want a soul to perish, but reconsiders, devising means so that one who has been cast off may not perish utterly"? Likewise Ezekiel, speaking in the words of God, says: "Much labor has been sweated over, yet her great rust has not gone out of her, nor has your abominable uncleanness gone out through fire; for I wanted to cleanse you, and you were not cleansed of your filth." See, God not only wants man to be saved, but sweats with much labor to cleanse him. Yet, for justice's sake, the physician's care does not bring about the result by itself, because it waits for the will of the one who is to be cleansed. Likewise: "The bellows have failed; in vain has the smelter smelted, for your wickedness has not been consumed." When you hear of the bellows and the smelter's work, understand pure metal corrupted by a counterfeit admixture and spoiled from its natural purity. If man is driven to death by God's impulse and will, why again in Ezekiel does he speak reproachfully and as though grieving: "Why will you die, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord. Turn back and live"? And how does he drive to death, as you blasphemously say, those whom he invites to life not only with a nod of command but with the feeling of one who pleads? Likewise: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked should turn from his way and live." Let the one whom the Lord calls to return recognize that his return lies in his own power. "As I live, says the Lord": so that the guilty may not doubt his pardon, the judge confirms his clemency even by interposing a kind of oath. And in the words of the apostle Peter the will of the most kind Creator is made known: "The Lord does not delay his promise, but is patient for your sake, not wanting any to perish, but all to return to repentance." Repentance is pressed upon the sinner, so that in the granting of mercy justice may also have its place. "But he is patient," he says, toward man's amendment, because what he desires impatiently he awaits patiently. Likewise, according to Luke: "And as he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying: They will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation."

Here the heretics must be pinned down. If the Lord had shut off the way of salvation to those who were going to perish, then he wept falsely over their destruction. But if, as is evident, he grieved over their perdition with real sorrow, he showed that what was lacking was not his will toward man but man's consent to his will. What wonder if he sheds tears for man's salvation, when he was soon to shed his blood? Likewise in Matthew: "Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!" Here the divine word does two things. For when he says, "How often I wanted, and you would not," the goodness of purpose in God and the freedom of choice in man are expressed. And by saying, "Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you," he declares that he wanted to save them, while plainly setting out the reasons for which he ought to have denied them salvation. In this passage two things are shown: in the servant, the wickedness of a bloodthirsty mind; in the Lord, the indulgence of a most kind will. If God wants man to perish, how is it that the prophet Micah also says: "I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: surely to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God"? When he says, "and what the Lord requires of you: surely to do justice," he would not be demanding a will ready to do good works if he had not given it. You see that, just as it belongs to God to call and exhort, so it is left to man's obedience to follow.

BOOK TWO.
AGAINST THE IMPIOUS ASSERTION THAT PHARAOH'S HEART WAS HARDENED BY GOD.

Here let us examine the meaning of holy Scripture more carefully and ask the objector what he thinks: was Pharaoh hardened by the Lord willingly or against his will? If he was unwilling [?], you certainly assign the blame for the hardening to Pharaoh himself; but if he was hardened against his will, you accuse God, who hardened him, of injustice. For what justice would there be in God himself punishing the man he himself had hardened? But since the Lord himself speaks to him and says, "Why will you not let my people go?" or

"How long will you refuse to submit to me?", here we see from the divine testimony that Pharaoh's will was free. This is the sense in which the Lord says, "I will harden Pharaoh": by allowing him to defy me through the ten plagues, which I take away when Moses entreats me. "I," he says, "will harden Pharaoh's heart." We sometimes use this same kind of expression in ordinary speech among ourselves. Sometimes we reproach stubborn servants with our own mildness, saying: "My patience has made you thoroughly wicked; my leniency has fed your malice and arrogance; my indulgence has made you defiant; by overlooking your faults I encouraged your heart to harden against me." In this way what bears witness to virtue in the master's goodness becomes a vice in the servant's wickedness.

Now the divine word says: "And when Pharaoh saw that relief had been granted, he made his heart heavy." This passage states quite plainly that the relief he was granted hardened Pharaoh's heart. For when it says "he hardened his heart," the verb is not passive but active. Do you want to know how God's forbearance became the occasion of his hardened mind? This same Pharaoh, caught up in the ten plagues, softened when he was struck and grew heavy again when he was let off. So divine severity bent the impious man, while divine goodness hardened him; and, to show that he had free choice, he let the people go when God chastised him and called them back when God spared him. See how heavenly gentleness hardens a rebellious spirit: when the scourges come he grows mild, when they withdraw he grows insolent. Recognize the reason for the hardening and the force of his own will. The Hebrew people, whom he now orders to leave because of the affliction laid on him, and now forbids to leave because the plagues have eased, he finally urges and even forces to depart in haste when the plagues press hard upon him. So he is not hardened by God's great power; he becomes contemptuous through God's great patience. In short, amid the alternating turns of punishment and respite, he is humbled when scourged, lifted up when his prayer is heard, insolent when set free, obedient when afflicted. And the will he showed at the last proves that the children of Israel, whom he is known to have released after the tenth plague, he could have released after the first. And when, in the midst of his chastisements, he declares, "You are just, O Lord, but I and my people are wicked," he testifies against his own conscience that he was corrupted not by God but by his own will. And do you presume to claim that God was harsh or unjust toward Pharaoh, when that sacrilegious man himself could not deny that God was just and merciful toward him?

Does a Christian complain that God is cruel, when even an impious man confesses him to be merciful? The dispensation of heavenly mercy, then, does in human beings what the pouring of rain does on the earth. When abundant rain falls, ground that has been cultivated and tamed multiplies its yield of crops, while ground left wild and untilled is filled with useless weeds and briars. So one and the same rain produces two different and opposite results, depending on the care or the neglect of cultivation, as we read: "For land that drinks the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those who till it, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned." See how land, under one and the same rain, now sprouts thorns and thistles, now brings forth fruit fit for blessing. In the same way, while God's mercy waits and spares, the obedient man is corrected and the impenitent is hardened.
II. THAT GOD'S FOREKNOWLEDGE DOES NOT FORCIBLY DRIVE HUMAN WILLS EITHER TO WHAT IS RIGHT OR TO ITS OPPOSITE.

Those who claim that God's foreknowledge and predestination give rise to human actions misunderstand them. First we must see what depends on what, or proceeds from what. A man does not do whatever he is going to do because the authority of the one who foreknows will compel him; rather, it is the freedom and will of the man foreknown that give God's foreknowledge its particular content. So the cause of sinning is not imposed on a man by any force in foreseeing; rather, the order of foreknowledge arises from the merits that human beings will go on to have. The general foreknowledge which God has of the state of the whole world springs from his power; but with regard to man's condition, the particular content and kinds of foreknowledge are drawn from observing human action.

But at this point you answer God and say: "O Lord, how could I lay hold of the good, when you foreknew that I would be evil?" It is not so. What God wills is one thing; what God permits is another. He wills the good and permits evil; he foreknows both. What is just he assists by his goodness; what is unjust he permits for the sake of free choice. That he gives grace comes from him; that he foreknows the offense comes from you. And this is why, with regard to the wicked, he is found ceaselessly forbidding the very things he has foreseen. He would never command men's corrupt inclinations to turn to better things if he knew that they could not be changed. And so divine providence will rightly answer you: "O man, I did not make you such as I foreknew you would be. I formed you good, according to the law of my justice, and I warned you not to follow evil; I foresaw you as evil because of the wickedness your own will would go on to choose." Where the complaint reveals not compulsion to sin but consent to it, the blame lies not with the maker but with the transgressor. "If you look to your maker, O man," he says, "you could have been good; if you look to the one who foreknew you, it was you who, by the course of your deeds, compelled me to foreknow evil of you."

But you come back and say: "The foreknowledge and predestination of human acts and merits fix and set in motion their causes beforehand." It is not so. Rather, the kind of foreknowledge is derived from the source in the human will. But that some are led by the perversity of their thinking to suppose that their acts originate in foreknowledge comes from a vice in their own minds and from incorrigible obstinacy, as they pretend to struggle against their passions and think they cannot do what in fact they do not want to do. They call their habit of sinning a law of unchangeable evil. But you still say that the works and wills of human beings begin from the nod and impulse of heavenly foreknowledge. It is not so. Recognize rather that God's foreknowledge takes its starting point from the material of human acts. What God is to foreknow and foreordain about us, as far as the future is concerned, depends on a man's progress or decline.

Take this example, in which God's foreknowledge changes in response to human action. Death is announced to King Hezekiah as he lies sick, in the grim word of a truthful prophet, who declares: "Set your house in order, for tomorrow you will die." But he turned to weeping and set his house in order, for he humbled his soul. He recognizes the prophet as a man of proven holiness, yet despair is driven back by hope: prayer countermands the oracle, supplication undoes the decree, full faith overcomes the truth of the word, and the extreme weakness of a man in tears overcomes the inescapable cause of the death that had been announced. Human frailty humbles itself, and the divine sentence suffers a kind of violence, as it is written: "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence." He would certainly have died had he not, in his terror, made supplication. Choose which you prefer: either admit that a fixed necessity was changed, or convict the truth of having lied.
III. THAT TO FOREKNOW IS ONE THING AND TO PREDESTINE ANOTHER.

The Apostle says: "Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son." To foreknow is one thing, to predestine another. Foreknowledge knows in advance what is to be done; afterward predestination sets down what is to be repaid. The one foresees merits, the other foreordains rewards. Foreknowledge belongs to power, predestination to justice. Foreknowledge rests on another's act, predestination on its own judgment; the one reveals the crime, the other condemns it; the one is the witness, the other the judge. Once the one has announced the cause, the other then announces the sentence. By foreknowledge what is ours is disclosed; by predestination what belongs to it [?] is prepared. Thus predestination decides nothing unless foreknowledge has first examined the case. The power of the eye plays the part of foreknowledge: whatever presents itself to its sight, that it will see. Is it believed to have done what it is known to have detected? Since the eyes see not what they themselves produce within but what is presented to them from without, if they happen to see someone sinning, the shameful act will, I think, be judged to belong not to the one who sees but to the one who commits it. So the guilt of every offense will belong not to the one who foreknows but to the one who is foreknown.

So too God foresees, before a man's day, the things that are to be done not by himself but by the man. And just as an existing object brings it about [?] that the eye's gaze beholds it, whereas the eye does not cause the thing to be seen to come into being, so God's foreknowledge does not require the things that will follow from human merits to happen, but runs ahead of them as they are about to happen. And since it is the custom of the sacred Scriptures to disclose the truth of what they assert by taking up some likeness or other (as we read that the kingdom of heaven is compared now to a grain of mustard seed, now to the leaven of the woman in the Gospel, now to a net cast into the sea, and many other such things), so we too, wishing to distinguish future things, gather the nature of foreknowledge from this illustration [?]. But if to foreknow is to compel, is the one who foresees the sinner therefore himself the cause of the sin? God foreknows adultery: does he therefore himself set the bones and marrow ablaze with the fires of obscene frenzy? God foreknows a murderer: does he himself suggest bestial impulses to disordered senses, does he himself sharpen the sword of a bloodthirsty mind to carry out the crime? He foreknows the impious man: does he therefore himself goad a madman's spirit to profane sacrifices? Must we really believe that he is the author of the very things he avenges? And amid all this, is he to be judged as forcing the consent of a captive will toward evil, he who did not permit even the devil to compel the unwilling? It is the will that commits the offense; it is the will that merits help.

But you say: "I find a case where grace alone works without any partnership of the human will: in Bethlehem the whole company of the innocents obtained so blessed a death by God's predestination alone." It is not so. It might perhaps then have been the work of grace alone if the shedding of innocent blood had not intervened. But if the innocents then had one and the same cause, why are not all infants saved there? For every age of the other sex is excluded from the glory of that time. If the force of predestination creates a particular condition for each individual, why do all these boys, born at different times, on different days and in different months, obtain one and the same happiness? But if the principle of election operates indiscriminately across the human race, why is every girl excluded from this gift? Here, then, with no lot of any decree at work, death is inflicted on the boys through the devil's rage, while the blessedness of that death is conferred for God's honor. So predestination did not consign them to death; rather, the occasion of the cause consecrated them. This slaughter of little ones, therefore, was ordered not by God's arrangement but by the impiety of the enemy. But God, who makes good use even of human evils, works the glory of the slain out of the crime of the slayer. The inventor of malice arranges things against us, but the author of goodness reworks hostile designs for the better.
IV. AGAINST THEIR SAYING: "HE IS MERCIFUL TOWARD THOSE WHOM HE WINS, AND JUST TOWARD THOSE WHOM HE ABANDONS," SINCE HE SHOWS HIMSELF BOTH MERCIFUL TOWARD THE WICKED AND JUST TOWARD THE GOOD AS WELL.

If God disposes man's condition not by equity but by power, as impiety blasphemously claims, then perhaps the one who knocked is shut out and the one who did not seek is drawn in. And so he will not appear to have been merciful toward the saved, to whom he did not grant that they should merit mercy by their service; nor could he be thought just toward the lost, who are driven away from mercy without any crime of their own. And if both are guilty by nature, justice will be endangered in the one who, unworthy, is chosen without merit, and mercy in the other, who is consigned to perdition without any judgment on his sin. For by what mercy is the idle man honored, by what justice is the harmless man condemned? So while such a view ignorantly takes away man's freedom, it is shown impiously to deny God's justice. If you say that he is merciful only in the one he wins and just only in the one who is lost, you will flatly deny both virtues in both persons. For there will be no equity in the one case if he chooses someone untested, and no goodness in the other if he destroys someone undeserving.

We, however, confess that in God's works these two goods are joined together in an inseparable embrace, as we read: "Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord"; and again: "The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy"; and again: "The Lord is merciful and compassionate and just." For he is merciful even toward the lost, since he seeks out and invites those who stray and long bears with those who sin. And just as he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and sends rain on the just and the unjust, so he has filled both alike with the light of reason, clothed them with the honor of his image, and called them all to the grace of redemption. Was he really not merciful toward the man on whom he heaped so much, the man he will judge for mercy neglected and lost? It is a lesser task to show that toward those he wins he is just as well as merciful: just, I say, toward those he receives when they return, those he does not abandon when they labor, those he makes worthy of freedom when they serve faithfully. The heretic, however, denies that God is merciful toward the wicked because he does not believe that an abundance of salvation was offered to those who slip into death; and he does not affirm that God is just toward the good because he thinks nothing is bestowed on them in return for humble devotion. He is merciful, then, because he gives even the wicked an understanding of reason and an inclination to goodness; just, because he sets a reward before the obedient; just, because he saves no one against his will.

So the Apostle splendidly joins the duty of labor to the gift of grace when he says: "The farmer who labors ought to receive a share of the crops." See how, by a wonderful exchange, the divine and the human are joined together. Labor belongs to obedience, but the fruit of labor to grace. And again: "Each will receive his own wage according to his own labor"; while the Lord says in the Gospel: "When you have done these things, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done." Notice that he does not exclude zeal for work but requires the humble submission of the one who works; he does not refuse the labor of service but instills humility of mind. The fault, then, lies not in the work, as you most ignorantly suppose when you think labor is to be shunned, but in the heart. So I will labor with all my strength, but whatever I receive from heavenly generosity I will credit to grace, not to my own effort; I will call it a kindness, not a payment; I will declare it a gift, not a debt, a reward freely given, not a repayment. Thus, when we do something out of duty, we can in no way charge it to God's account, because we are only paying what we owe. But do not begrudge the divine goodness if a work that I have done well with its help, or even what I have received, I should lose [?]. In this way their preceding evils allow them neither to be converted nor to be healed.
V. AGAINST THEIR SAYING THAT THE ONE WHO PERISHED WAS NOT SO MUCH UNWILLING AS UNABLE TO BE SAVED, ACCORDING TO WHAT WE READ: "AND THEY COULD NOT BELIEVE."

Among these passages, John the evangelist records: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart.” At this point the words, ending as they do, sound as though a necessity of not believing seems to be laid on them against their will. But the order of the reading shows in what follows that the cause, or the fault, of their unbelief arose from themselves, for it says: “Nevertheless many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue. For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God.” Here he shows plainly, as we also read of Simon, that the power of believing had been given even to the unfaithful. In them, just as the capacity to believe was present, so the will to confess was lacking. That they believe is the bounty of grace; that they do not join open profession to what they believe is the perversity of the mind. And in them this is fulfilled: “But from him who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.”

See how malice, once mixed in, corrupted the good of will and of faith, as the Lord himself says in another place in the same Gospel: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” You see, then, that just as the truth is hidden when the causes are suppressed, so obscurity is removed when they are made plain. That obscurity seems to draw somewhat thicker clouds over Isaiah's testimony, when he asserts that those whom their own wickedness had made deaf and blind were blinded by God, lest perhaps their heart should turn to God and they be healed. So, setting aside for a little what Matthew expressed more openly, let us look more deeply, in keeping with the severity of the saying itself, which strikes the reader's ear rather harshly in the prophet's words, into why the Lord is thought in this place not to want them to be healed. It is this: lest, having undergone a merely momentary conversion, they should abuse the benefits conferred on them, and so, by relapsing into sickness, be shown to have neglected and rejected the medicine they had received, like the man to whom the Lord himself says: “See, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.”

Notice that the wicked man is weighed down all the more by the goodness of being healed. Thus Pharaoh is found to have mocked the mercy of God: as often as God wished to heal him, when, given over to the plagues, he came to his senses, turned, and humbled himself, so often did God find him worse after the kindness of his clemency. Why, I ask, does he hold back from healing these people? Surely so that they may not become like the one sown on rocky ground, that is, the one who receives the word with joy for a moment, who believes for a while and in the time of temptation falls away. What is it to receive a momentary healing? It is to believe for a while and, in the time of temptation, to fall away through the faithlessness of one's mind, and to wither at the slight heat of temptation because the root is weak. Let us look at those whom he tried to heal, and for whom it did little good because of the unbelief that followed. See: from that servant in the Gospel, weighed down with great debts and sicknesses of soul, the ten thousand talents that seemed to have been forgiven him are exacted, with torments added, because of the crime of his own malice. Here too we must note how what has been gained is lost and how benefits already conferred are revoked.

We also read that the man from whom the unclean spirit had been driven out was healed for a time. Of him the divine word says: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it passes through dry places seeking rest and finds none. Then it says: I will return to my house from which I came. And when it comes it finds it empty, swept and adorned”, that is, emptied of virtues and filled with vanities. “Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” See, here is one to whom the healing conferred on him was of no profit: with evils multiplied, a harmful sickness settled on him and grew. And in another place, the man who, after receiving knowledge of the truth, that is, after the truth had given him the care of salvation, counted as unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, that is, by which he was healed, is said on the apostle's testimony to deserve heavier punishments. So grace is turned into guilt unless watchfulness follows it. But in these matters the evangelist Matthew, by referring the hardened heart, the stopped ears and the closed eyes to the fault of man as the reason why they were not healed, taught the point with a clearer sense and a more lucid argument when, I say, he wrote: “The heart of this people has grown fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes.” Does it not seem to you that, as if answering those who ask why seeing they do not see and hearing they do not understand, he at once gave a clear account of the reasons why they neither see nor understand? It is because they refused to hear and see, that is, to understand and obey. “For”, he says, “not all obey the gospel”, since “all day long he stretches out his hands to a people that does not believe and that contradicts.” So too the Lord himself already says: “I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have despised me”; and again: “For they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters.” And in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what Paul was saying, blaspheming the way of the Lord”; and again: “Paul was pressing on with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. But when they contradicted and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said: Your blood be on your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” “When they contradicted”, it says, “and blasphemed.” See how the physician applies remedies and the sick man refuses them. Blessed Stephen too rebukes their hardness with equal authority, saying: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.” See why they cannot see: because they resist the Holy Spirit and, having closed their eyes of their own accord, shut out the light of truth. What follows in the Gospel, then, where it says: “lest perhaps they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I heal them”, that is, that they cannot turn and be healed, is the vice of a hardened heart and the punishment of sin. “Lest”, he says, “they turn and I heal them.” He is not here refusing healing to those who want it; he is declaring that he does not want, that is, ought not, to heal those who oppose him. The physician's goodness is most ready to give the remedy, but the sick man's lack of self-control resists it. For whoever thinks it should be understood to mean that he did not want to heal them acquits man and condemns the Maker. So no one is shut out from God's benefits; rather, he must first be judged for the benefits he has neglected.
VI. WHAT IS MEANT BY THE WORDS: “FOR WHEN THEY HAD NOT YET DONE ANYTHING GOOD OR EVIL”

But they try to squeeze into the narrow confines of a pagan decree of fate that meaning of the apostle where he says: “For this is the word of promise: About this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son. And not only so, but also Rebecca, when she had conceived by one man, our father Isaac. For when they were not yet born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God's purpose according to election might stand, not from works but from him who calls, it was said that the elder will serve the younger, as it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” In these words the impiety of a pagan conviction wants us to understand that God, without any weighing of evil and good such as a governor would make, not by the order of one who rules but by the right of one who simply dominates, makes the one worthy of his love and the other of his hatred, takes up the one with favor and shuts out the other by decree; and that between two men equally lost no account is taken of effort or of devotion, but one is taken up without reason though he has done no duties, and the other is condemned without distinction. And so, since in neither of them is there any ground for merit or for guilt, the very basis of the judgment to come is wholly taken away.

But if such an unworthy confusion of things is foreign even to the understanding of the human mind, let us inquire more carefully what befits divine justice as the apostle explains it. Placed between two peoples, as teacher of Jews and Gentiles, when he says “the elder will serve the younger”, in the elder the arrogance of Judea is rejected, and in the younger the faith of the Gentiles is chosen. So the man who does not so much follow the meaning of Holy Scripture and adapt himself to it as try to drag Holy Scripture violently toward his own understanding and presumptuously bend it to his own purposes draws the clouds of ignorance over himself. Ignoring the sense of what precedes and what follows, he persuades himself, as far as his grasp allows, of something the apostle never set out to speak about at all. But if you go back to the beginning of the very chapter under discussion, you will escape every ambiguity without any difficulty. If the teacher of the Gentiles had begun to treat of the origin of men, and had said that the whole course of a man's life was fixed in advance from his origin and was subject to necessity rather than entrusted to free choice, because the Lord of all, by a nod of his power and a violent decree, left some to perdition and chose others for salvation, then perhaps a wicked conviction could claim this coloring, as though following the lines of the text. But since the apostle weaves together God's promises and the calling of the Gentiles with examples drawn from far back, and strives in every way to curb the presumption of the Jews, who shamelessly puffed themselves up over the works of the law, he does not establish a fatal decree in the origin of the elder ones, Ishmael or Esau, but shows the election of the younger people in the blessing of Isaac and Jacob. And therefore he set the younger before the elder not as if by God's power but according to his justice, for he foresaw the impiety of the Jews just as he foresaw the obedience of the Gentiles. So when he says: “For when they had not yet done anything good or evil, not from works but from him who calls, it was said that the elder will serve the younger”, it was indeed said from him who calls, but it is plain that it was said not of people to be compelled or repelled, but of those who would believe and those who would not, so that, while divine justice remains consistent with itself, it rests with man's will either to reject or to keep the commandments. So when you hear “but from him who calls, it was said”, understand one who invites, not one who compels. Again, when he says “not from works”, he is asserting, concerning them, not the works of the law, which certainly had not yet come, but that even before the law the gifts of divine mercy and generosity were in force. “Not from works”, he says. You hear that the works of the law are set aside, and on that account, with foolish understanding, you believe that, even among those living under the law of grace, some can be saved without the works of grace, while others, even with works, are shut out from the door of salvation by a natural bond and a law of fate that forbids it. “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” How, according to this interpreter of perverse understanding, is a heavenly sentence pronounced here concerning those not yet born? One not yet begotten can be neither guilty nor beloved. One not yet brought into the light merits nothing; but just as their manner of life still lay in the future, so a future offense by one who foresees, and a future election, are foretold. For just as divine providence knows how to judge deeds already done, so it does not know how to prejudge deeds yet to be done.

So let no one think that a necessity of differing merits was fixed in advance for the brothers before they were born, since the prophet Malachi records this of them after the warfare of their life was over, and pronounces a divine judgment, with manifest fairness, on their past state: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” What wonder is it if justice loves innocence and rejects iniquity, since for justice even future things are already done? But because the younger is by law set before the elder, and Jacob is loved while his brother is passed over, obscurity arises for those who are somewhat slower. They suppose that the testimony of love and hatred was given about the brothers before they were born, while the plain reasons why the one displeased and the other pleased are passed over in silence. In these two, then, no laws of nature are fixed in advance for men; rather, the statutes of justice concerning the faith of the Gentiles and the unbelief of the Jews are being related. For in this place it is not the persons of the brothers individually, according to the letter, that are described, but the causes and mysteries of things, as the Lord says: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly.” If a fixed law of origin were being treated here, what need was there to bring in the age of the elder and the younger, which had nothing to do with the matter, except that among the stock of the Jews, in the calling of two peoples, the younger is always preferred to the elder? Yet within this division of parties many are chosen from among the rejected Jews and many rejected from among the chosen Gentiles, so that you may understand that in both peoples the just Judge regards not a decree but merits.

But you say: When they had not yet done anything good or evil, they were already assigned to their predetermined portions. What wonder is it if he marked out in advance the end of those whose actions he foresaw? And so, just as it was certain that they would order the course of their lives by their own choice, so by God's power they are foreknown, and by his justice they are foreordained. All this is foretold about them, not predetermined. In Jacob, then, the faithful people is portrayed; in Esau the unbelieving people is signified. Of both he says: “What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have attained righteousness, the righteousness that is from faith; but Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, has not attained to the law of righteousness. Why? Because they pursued it not from faith but as if from works. For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling.” When it is said “not from works”, you see that the works of the law are set aside, and that obedience opened the way to mercy for the Gentiles, while for the Jews their prior iniquity and unbelief prepared their stumbling. “Not from works”, he says, “but from him who calls, it was said.” He does not say that they were empty of works of their own, but denies that they were saved by the works of the law. Far be it from anyone to think that a condemnation of origin is set forth here, where the kindness of the one who calls and the humility of the one who obeys are proclaimed, and where a teaching for all impresses the riches of faith and instills the light of belief. So let no doctrine of iniquity, which would say that part of the human race was condemned in its very creation, insert itself into this passage. The history of Genesis has clearly set out the reasons why God loved Jacob and hated Esau, so that you may understand that it was not without examination of their works, nor without a clear reason, that God declared Esau worthy of his hatred and Jacob worthy of his love. Plainly there appeared in Jacob's life evident causes which [?] the judgment
