VIII. (AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT ADAM PERISHED ENTIRELY).
[?] “its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it.” Under this law of his ordinance he did not set sin over man, but placed it beneath him.

See: the most loving Governor, wishing his creature to remain noble even when brought low after the fall, commands that man's will be not the servant but the mistress of all passion and desire. He placed in man's hand either friendship with the seducer or rejection of him, and set it within his judgment. He seems indeed to have left to man's choice the desire for either kind of action, but only so that the freedom to do evil might become the glory of doing good. “But its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it.” No necessity of sinning confines the one to whose discernment it is entrusted to master sin by a superior freedom. But degenerate is the mind which, though with God's help it can win victory over sin, prefers to offend God and be the slave of sin.

Since this is so, what followed the first man's transgression was not the death of free choice but its weakness, not impossibility but difficulty, with toil set before it. Abel too merited to please the divine sight through the good implanted by God in all men, that is, through the disposition of his own will. This man, to whom the perfection of a spotless life gave the name “the just”, by whose teaching would he have become a follower of righteousness, had not the law written within him taught him? Or how would he have known to choose, from the fat portions and the firstfruits, sacrifices that would please God and be taken up by fire from heaven, unless faith, which had made him a lover of virtues, had inspired him? As we read: “By faith Abel offered a greater sacrifice than Cain, God bearing witness to his gifts.” He could never have obtained this unless the servant's obedience had been joined to the Lord's gift. And do you judge that, by God's ordinance, he has nothing of his own, when God bears witness to his devotion? Do you see that the good of believing is not a new privilege but an ancient one, and that at the very beginnings of the world, as it was taking shape, the mind of man was endowed by the supreme Author with faith, just as it was with understanding and reason? So already then he gave the soul knowledge of himself, when he deigned to entrust his image to it.
IX. AFTER WHOSE IMAGE AND LIKENESS THE FIRST MAN WAS CREATED.

But you say: why do you link the image of God with freedom of choice, when that excellent Creator, who was to be the Redeemer in the ages that followed, made man rather after the image that he was going to take from humanity through the Virgin? Many put this view forward, but every argument strips it bare, because the beginnings of what comes first can in no way put on the image of something much later. How could he who was created first receive the likeness of one not yet created? Of the two, it would be easier to believe that the first Adam passed on his image to the second Adam, as order and time would require. But it could not possibly be that he who was formed so many ages before should be called the image of a substance that did not yet exist. Nor could one accept the ill-considered claim that, as they say, the person of the most ancient first-formed man came before the author of his likeness, who was still to be born of the Virgin.

Add to this that it would greatly lower the glory of man's first innocence if, while still spotless, he were fashioned on the pattern of the one who was to heal the stains of the man who would sin. Then, though transgression did not yet exist, the form of the future intercessor would already display the guilt of transgression. It was not fitting, therefore, that the finished and perfect creature should be made after the image of him through whom the lost would have to be restored. Otherwise, under the name of the physician who was to come, the downfall of the one who would be tripped up would seem to be foretold at the very moment of that happy beginning. It is more reasonable, then, that in man, to whom God hands over in this very likeness something that belongs to grace, not to nature, the name 'image' should rather be given to what is received from the one who is prior and higher. The likeness should be judged to have been conferred more fully from the truth itself, the truth that the Father shares by right with his Son by nature. Next, we must note this too with special care: in the first age our Lord Jesus Christ conferred better things from what is his, but in the second he took on lesser things from what is ours. And so when he made us out of nothing, as Maker he set his own image upon us; but when he restored us after we were lost, as Restorer he took the form of a servant, as the apostle says: "Taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man."

If we were formed after the outward appearance of man, in whose members are sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, what honor or grace would there be in sharing an image that we know we have largely in common with the beasts? Those who think that the incorporeal Trinity made the first man on the pattern of the one who was to be taken from Mary are therefore gravely mistaken. Neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was to be clothed in the garment of flesh and the bearing of a man, as though he arranged the features of the first man and shaped his limbs after his own appearance and handiwork, as after his image, so that he could say: "Let us make man in the image and likeness that we are going to take from this Virgin." Whatever the Trinity bestows on man in common, then, derives from the likeness of the Godhead. Indeed, even if the Son of God alone had made man, it still could not be said that the first man received the image of the second Adam. But since the united Trinity says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," mingling singular with plural and plural with singular, and again, "And God made man in his image and likeness; in the image of God he made him," you read so often that man was created in the image of God. By what authority, then, do you presume to assert against the divine words that he was made after the form of a servant? Since this image is conferred by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, beyond doubt the one divinity of the three persons granted the first man the dignity of its own image.

This being so, you will have no doubt that man still possesses freedom of his own will, though it is weakened, if you consider the first grace with which God honored him. Man is called the image of God because the Truth graciously and generously implanted justice in him, Reason implanted wisdom, and the Everlasting implanted eternity. It comes from the image of God that he understands, that he has a sense for what is right, and that he distinguishes between evil and good by weighing them with judgment. And since God is goodness, mercy, patience and justice, the more just and patient anyone is found to be, the more like God he is shown to be; for this likeness is possessed not in features but in virtues. That is why it is said of God that he is subtle, simple and pure. He is simple because nothing is added to him from outside and nothing is conferred on him from elsewhere; in him are virtue, essence and substance. So God is what he has, whereas man does not have these gifts unless he receives them. Since God is just and is justice, is merciful and is mercy, is kind and is kindness, man can be just but cannot be justice; he can be merciful but cannot be mercy; he can be kind but cannot be kindness, because he has these things not by nature but by bounty. For example, God is gold, while man can be seen as a gilded vessel. What is nature in God is grace in man, and what is shown to be unbegotten in God is created in man. So by this reasoning man's condition appears rather to be twofold, since these things are implanted in him in such a way that they are often separated from him and taken away.

Those who think that justice and the other virtues are the substance of the soul are therefore mistaken. The soul can somehow go on existing in its nature, with its vital vigor, without them, and the devil too is known to remain in his nature without them. They are plainly shown to be added, since they are stripped away when sins come between. Only free choice and immortality, which are implanted even in the wicked, are not taken away, although the dignity and blessedness of immortality can be taken away. As far as freedom of choice and immortality are concerned, then, even the wicked can have the image of God, though it is discolored by them and in them; but only the good can have the likeness. This being so, since men were so endowed with the image and likeness of God that many even deserved to be called sons of God, we must touch briefly, even if only with a few examples, on how many, before the law of the letter, entered the vestibule of salvation under the teaching of the law of nature, which, as we have said, is the first grace of God, to be led through Christ into the inner sanctuary of life itself.

Seth [?] too was put in Abel's place, being like him in character and merit. How could he have rejected his brother's profane ways and chosen better ones, unless understanding and reason had directed him onto the right path? With these as his guide he passed on holy traditions and praiseworthy teachings to his descendants like an inheritance, so that for many generations they were reckoned under the name of angels or sons of God. Who would doubt that countless households of his were pleasing to God, endowed with freedom of choice, and that some were saved from among the nations as well? Of these, only a very few are named in Holy Scripture, but these are illustrious and perfect, to give light to the world. How could Enoch have walked with God or pleased God, unless the law poured into his heart had enlightened him by its hidden teaching so much that, having no taste for anything earthly, he was wondrously caught away from the earth as God took him up? Since he surpassed everyone else of that earliest age in the merit of his faith, he showed clearly that faith itself had been given to him along with the law of nature, as we read: "By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death. For before he was taken up he had the testimony that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God. For whoever comes to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him." God would not bestow a reward on man unless he were sought with willing devotion and effort, and unless he had given man something of his own with which he could please him. And when Scripture says, "For before he was taken up he had the testimony that he pleased God," there is no doubt that the life is examined first and then election follows. In the doctrine of predestination, the error that creeps in will easily be avoided if one asks about the cause that comes first. He becomes, then, the rewarder of those who seek him. And he who gave the means by which he could be sought is absent from the one who does not seek him, to that man's great guilt.

The perfect justice of Noah also made clear what kind of law, and how great a law, man received from God at his first creation, for as a follower of virtue he cultivated in himself, with particular zeal, the gifts of faith that are common to all. In his time all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, and condemnation would not have followed if transgression arising from man's choice had not come first. Just as guilt deserves punishment, so punishment, which the Ruler inflicts in fairness, testifies to guilt. And when the divine word says, "All flesh had corrupted its way," it attributes the iniquities of that time not to an imposed decree but to voluntary depravity. Beyond doubt, then, the heavenly dispensation would not have given the law of the letter if transgression had not violated the law of nature to the point of bringing on the wrath of the Flood. So this law of Moses, which is believed to be the first, is in fact the second.

The most blessed bishop Augustine also shows, in a very learned discourse, that the work of the natural law was written in human hearts. He says: "Both run together in this channel and torrent of the human race: the evil drawn from the parent, and the good bestowed by the Creator." And again: "No one's vice is so contrary to nature that it wipes out even the last traces of nature. That is why even the ungodly think about eternal things and lay down laws worthy of praise even in this present age, and rightly blame many things and rightly praise many things in human conduct. By what rules, after all, do they judge these things, if not by natural rules, in which they see how each person ought to live, even if they themselves do not live that way?" The apostle testifies to this still more plainly when he says to the Romans: "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who hold back the truth in injustice, because what is known of God is plain to them, for God has shown it to them. For since the creation of the world his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made, his eternal power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man." Ungodliness would not have felt the wrath of God if the will had not departed from the law of God. And when he says, "because what is known of God is plain in them, for God has shown it to them," he clearly teaches that, through an inner teaching written on the pages of the mind, the knowledge of God ought to have been plain to them, and that the Creator could have been known through the magnificence of creation. They would certainly not be without excuse before God unless they had had, both outwardly and inwardly, ample means of grasping the truth; and so the apostle adds: "For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God." He condemns the ungodly, then, also on account of their understanding, because they abused it, and he charges that their injustice amounted to contempt for the Godhead.

And what else did the vast flood of that famous deluge demonstrate, if not the free choice of the human race, through the guilt of a condemned world? So the perfect justice of Noah both exposed and condemned the willful errors of that age, as we read: "By faith Noah, having received a revelation about things not yet seen, in reverent fear prepared an ark for the salvation of his household. Through it he condemned the world and became heir of the justice that comes through faith." Why did he condemn the world? Because the world's wickedness neglected to follow the example of justice. So he accuses the guilt of the disobedient, and, having himself pleased God through obedience, he proves that others too could have pleased him through their own effort. Certainly no decree of fate had any place in that age. Because the transgression that came first had been universal, the condemnation that followed was universal. How can you say that one is taken and another left? See how, apart from the family of the just man, the whole world is destroyed because iniquity compelled it. The particular decree that you assert is therefore ruled out by a general judgment, and he who is condemned for his wickedness is shown to have been able to do good.
X. On the claim that the law of nature perished in the first man and did not flourish in his descendants until the coming of the Savior.

But you say that the goods of nature ought not to be mentioned, since it is evident that before Christ's coming the Gentiles had no share at all in salvation. Whoever says that nature should not be praised for its goods surely does not know that the author of nature is himself the author of grace. Whoever most foolishly denies this places the good of nature outside God's workmanship, and supposes it to come either from some deity or from fate. But since the Creator is himself the Restorer, one and the same God is blessed in the praise of both works, and one and the same God is celebrated in the proclamation of both. So I rightly affirm the gift of each, because I know that I owe the fact that I was born to the same One to whom I owe the fact that I was reborn. For this reason I will not deny the Creator's gifts just because I lost them; yet I will not set the earlier gifts on a level with the later ones, because I received them restored and made better many times over. I will extol the benefits of the One who creates, but I will rank far above them the benefits of the One who redeems.

Nor shall I seem incautious in this either, if I declare that sometimes in God's dealings with us (not, indeed, at the very beginnings of our life, but only along the way) our will, by God's own ordering, goes before special graces that come from an added generosity. Let us ask the sacred Scriptures whether this is so. We read in the Gospel that the Lord says: "What do you want me to do for you?" And again: "Do you want to be made well?" You see that the gift of health is not granted unless the desire of the will is first asked about. Again, when someone comes to baptism, the will of the one approaching is asked about first, so that the grace of the One who regenerates may follow. And in the case of the centurion Cornelius, because his will went before grace, grace also went before his regeneration. Nothing here, I think, smacks of presumption, since I constantly affirm that I owe even the will itself to God, especially since in all its movements I attribute to the work of grace both the first beginnings and the final completion.

Abraham too, coming out from the midst of paganism, is not only called to salvation together with his whole household, but is even made the father of many nations by the testimony of Truth himself. That he is called comes from God's goodness; that he readily obeys comes from his own will. Job too could not have withstood the enemy pressing upon him without freedom of soul; rather, he joins greatness of heart with the help of his protector. And so the justice of the One who rewards shows the devotion of the one who fights. In spiritual warfare the struggle seems to belong to man's labor, just as the outcome is credited to God. Further, the fact that Job's friends came from the Gentiles points to a time when the law had not yet been given; and since it is recorded that Job, at the Lord's command, prayed for them and was heard, salvation beyond doubt is granted to these men too, while they were still living in paganism. Rahab, too, was so much of the Gentile nation that she prefigured the Church that was to be gathered from the Gentiles. She too is received into salvation with her whole household, by her faith [?], and of her we read: "By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with the unbelievers." Why are these people, who were outside the law, accused here as unbelievers, unless because they refused to keep the law of nature, to which faith is joined? Why is unbelief charged against them, unless because the ability to believe was ready at hand? So it is by reason of free choice that the believer is rewarded and the unbeliever condemned.

We read in the book of Genesis: "For the sins of the Amorites are not yet complete." The Lord foretells that the children of Israel will be humbled in the land of Egypt, and then brought out from there with signs and wonders to destroy the ungodly nations and to take possession of the dwelling places promised them. But he declares that this cannot happen until the nations he was going to hand over to them make room, by the greatness of their mounting sins, for the scourges they deserve, and by the weight of their completed iniquity compel the hand of final affliction to be stretched out against them. Where a multiplying of sins is waited for, the depravity of wills is exposed. He who, in fairness, passes sentence on a Gentile who was free from the law of commandments shows that the law of nature had been trampled underfoot; and at the same time the forbearance of the One who waits is shown to make plain the justice of the One who condemns. For no one who intends to punish by predestination allows a delay out of restraint. "The sins of the Amorites," he says, "are not yet complete." Since the cause of their destruction is said to lie in the fullness of their sins, the odium of a predetermined necessity is removed. Recognize in this passage the power of divine patience. The people of Israel, who were to be set free and to overthrow the ungodly nations, are kept in slavery for the time being, until the iniquity of the nations is complete. The wrath of judgment puts off vengeance for as long as the measure of sin is growing to its full heap, so that, with goodness and severity working together at one and the same time, the son might be set free on the one side and the enemy crushed on the other.
AGAINST THEIR CLAIM THAT BEFORE THE TIME OF GRACE THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE ONE GOD WAS NOT GRANTED TO THE GENTILES.

Those who say that the Gentiles could not have had knowledge of the one God before the Savior's coming are wallowing in a great depth of ignorance, since the Apostle declares that the Maker of the world could be known through the magnificence of what he made, saying: "What can be known about God is plain to them. For from the creation of the world his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made, his eternal power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse." How can you call them excusable on the ground that they were strangers to heavenly gifts, when God declares them inexcusable precisely because they are shown to have misused what they received, and could without difficulty have known the Maker's sublimity if they had questioned his work? It is far from all reason, and void of piety, to suppose that man has only recently been taught to know God, when the whole world has been his witness from the beginning of things. And so in the same letter the Apostle says: "For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires." So let no one think that man was imbued by some recent teaching for grasping God's law, when what he has by nature he received, surely, at the creation of the first man. "They exchanged," says the Apostle, "the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and serpents."

When the foolish man venerates base and unworthy things, he confesses that he owed worship by every means to worthier ones; and when he adores wood and stone, it was within his reach to have the sense to adore the Creator of things on earth and in heaven. For when a man acknowledges that something must be worshipped, his very understanding of worship exposes his offense against the Creator. How else, after all, did he have a sense of religion? He would without doubt have found God, had he been willing to apply a desire to seek him, since the Lord says: "Seek and you will find." For when the human mind opens its eyes to see, the light it seeks at once presents itself to the one who longs for it. So the law placed within taught veneration, but negligence and stubbornness did not deserve to find the truth. And therefore, when the heavenly handiwork prostrates itself before dead idols and senseless figures, it has done injury not only to its Maker but also to itself as his work; forgetful of its own noble birth, it has afflicted itself with shameful indignities, and from its very error it has received the penalty of error, as the Apostle says: "receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error." "And since they did not see fit to keep God in their knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind." Here the rebellious mind was corrupted of its own accord, not taken away by force. "Since they did not see fit," he says, "to keep God in their knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind." One who is abandoned for causes that came before is not crushed by fate but rejected by judgment.

But if you ask how the untaught nations, in their inborn savagery, came to have sin, how else than through a movement of the soul and the consent of the mind? After all, cattle and brute animals are entirely free from sin, because they know nothing of discernment and have no reason. You make man worse than a beast. For why do you leave sin to him from whom you take away choice? Or if you subject him to sin, do not deprive him of judgment. So let iniquity not lie to itself. He who knows hidden things knows what he has given to man in secret. And therefore, when anyone is rebuked and condemned by him for an evil deed, he is proved to have been able to do good. Great, then, is the power of the soul in either direction, since it is [?] over what is honorable and put to shame over what is dishonorable. And so it is said through the prophet: "His eyelids examine the sons of men; the Lord examines the righteous and the wicked." Why does the judge's [?] question me about sin, if what I commit is of his own decree? So he who fashioned the hearts of men one by one, as the hidden examiner, questions the ways of men and the merits of their consciences. But if you examine yourself too: whenever you wished to turn aside to the left, did not your trembling conscience warn you not to sin? Did not a sorrowful thought rebuke you like a hidden censor? And so men cannot hide from themselves, since their conscience bears witness to them and their thoughts among themselves accuse or even defend them.

Amid all this, if you ask where freedom of choice is located and where the will of man is set, where else than in understanding, in reason and in wisdom? This being so, you will first have to deny man wisdom and take away his reason before you can deprive him of free will. Therefore, whenever the soul, held captive within its own dwelling, contemplates some offense, the secret thoughts cry out against it and its own faculties forbid it from within; but the habit of sinning withdraws the strength to resist. But you come back and say that the wicked, and those who are being dragged to perdition, did not receive freedom of choice. First we must know that freedom of choice is endowed with a twofold service: it is ready now for one's salvation, now for one's perdition. But you object that freedom of the will belongs only to those who are to be set free and to those placed within the benefit of redemption. It is not so. Liberation belongs to the gift of grace and to the resolve of a life that consents; freedom of choice, however, is not a matter of added generosity but of nature. The former is either granted or preserved to those who seek it; the latter is conferred even on those who do not seek it. The former is bestowed on those who are reborn, the latter on those who are born. Freedom belongs to God's working alone; liberation also involves the service of man in subjection. The former is confirmed in the good; the latter is implanted even in the wicked. The former belongs to those who have been won and who persevere; the latter is available even to the lost. The former belongs to the Creator; the latter also to the one who obeys. The former is of power, the latter of mercy. The former is of origin and kind; the latter of gift and virtue.
XI. THAT THE GENTILES KNEW GOD BY NATURE.

The prophet Daniel, full of the Holy Spirit, knowing that God had placed in man's mind the desire for good or evil, addresses Nebuchadnezzar this way: "Therefore, O king, let my counsel be pleasing to you: redeem your sins with almsgiving, and your iniquities with mercy to the poor." "Redeem your sins," he says, "with almsgiving." Whatever can be redeemed cannot be seen as predetermined. Surely he is not shut out from healing who is urged to take a remedy. And at the same time choice is not denied to him from whom consent is demanded. He has not lost the function of a free mind who is shown to have been able to accept counsel. He is not found to be a stranger to salvation to whom the means of salvation is offered. And when the prophet offers him an occasion for obtaining pardon, he declares that the power of will is present in him.

Consider also that the Gentile Belshazzar is rebuked when the prophet says: "You have praised gods of silver and gold, of wood and stone, and the God in whose hand is your breath you have not praised." You see that this foreigner could both know and praise God, but would not. The prophet recalled that both the understanding of God and his worship are present in man, because he knew that the law of nature is in force without distinction within the mind of every man. And for this reason, when Daniel had revealed to the aforesaid King Nebuchadnezzar the meaning of his dream, the king, however profane, showed that he was not ignorant of God, saying: "Truly your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings." And who taught Darius too to think and speak of God in this way, if not the power of reason and of the law, together with Daniel? That God is appeased by conversion . . . [?]
XII. (ON THE NINEVITES).

[?] … how did it come to recognize that God's anger was conditional? That great city did not come to its senses through Jonah's teaching. It did not learn from his warnings that it should seek salvation. The prophet did not teach the people but terrified them. He did not promise mercy but announced an unchangeable sentence. And yet that city, as it is written, believed in hope against hope. It even promised itself remedies that had, in a sense, been denied to it, remedies that would greatly please God, even if it had sought ones that were promised.

The Lord sometimes withholds these remedies precisely so that, being won by greater effort, they may be held on to. At the same time, when a difficulty is set in the way of obtaining them and his generosity is hidden, faith is tested, eager seeking is exercised and love is brought into the open. All of this is done in man by an inner fire, planted by God and fed by man with the help of God's grace. So that nation showed that God, in the very order of his creation, placed within man the things that serve man's salvation. It showed that even before the gifts of the Redeemer, the Author's gifts were always alive in the rational creature. These gifts were indeed bestowed by the supreme Creator through nature, but they had to be confirmed through grace. Through grace, I say, in whose time the salvation of past ages was to be brought to completion, since neither the law of the letter nor the law of nature brought anything to perfection. In the Ninevites, then, the voice of the Lord was plainly displayed, full of clemency and goodness, when he says: "Suddenly I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to pluck up, destroy and root out. If that nation repents of its sin, I too will repent of the evil that I said I would do to it." The merciful judge wishes to change the decrees of the heavenly counsel by a holy falsehood if the guilty one hurries to apply a remedy to his sin. He lays the weight of condemnation on man unwillingly, for he shows the remedy of satisfaction and waits for the homage of diligent service. Therefore that perfect providence, which in this age delights in the exercise of virtues, judged it most fitting and most worthy of its wisdom to proceed in two stages. Man was created for the dignity of the sacred image, and providence would first test him here through struggles and contrition, and then fill him there with gifts and rewards. When the servant had shown obedience in his labour, the Lord would show justice in rewarding him. When human weakness had offered humble devotion, divine power would pour out a generosity beyond words.

We must therefore labour without ceasing, yet never withdraw from grace, and we must say: "O God, come to my help." The very word "help" requires the work of someone who labours. So the word "help" points to two parties: one who works and one who works with him, one who asks and one who promises, one who knocks and one who opens, one who seeks and one who rewards. This alone is ours: since our frailty leaves us unfit, we can at least please by persisting in seeking and knocking. What room will there be for the attentive care of a merciful God if the unworthy person deserves nothing and the idle bring nothing to it but wishes? Therefore, unless tireless obedience has first shown eagerness to comply, justice will have no ground on which to stand. That is why the divine word describes the farmer as one who rests his hope on his own labour, saying: "See, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, to receive the early and the late." What is the early, what the late? The early fruits are those we gain as the wages of our present service. The late fruits are those we shall gather in the recompense of that age, after our service is completed. The early fruits are faith and sincerity of heart, kindness, bodily self-control, contempt for evil, desire for good, the calm of gentleness and the purity of chastity. The late fruits are the gaining of immortal things, the inheritance of heavenly things and the possession of eternal things. Of these it is said: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." Of these it is also said, through apostles and martyrs: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us." So the early fruits lie in the virtues, the late fruits in the reward of the virtues. The early fruits are those that our deeds lay hold of here in keeping the commandments. The late fruits are those that our prayers will obtain there as rewards.

How greatly, then, would God be pleased if we built a wall, that is, a very strong barrier of supplication against what offends God. So did the one of whom we read: "For the blameless man hastened to pray for the people, holding up the shield of his service. He withstood the wrath and put an end to the calamity." And again: "Someone who would stand," he says, "set against me for this purpose, so that I would not destroy it." He who shows how his anger may be overcome is in a way already appeased even while he is angry. Consider, then, someone who says that the most powerful and most just Creator made man in such a way that one person is assigned to the left without any crime of his own, solely at the prompting of foreknowledge, while another is drawn to the right without his merits being examined. Such a person is caught openly asserting that the arrangements of both the Maker and the Judge are disordered or unjust.

But at this point let the hearer pay close attention. When the supreme Author was preparing to fashion man, when the supreme Author, I say, did so, four virtues stood by him to serve and counsel him in making man. Which four? Power, goodness, wisdom and justice. Consider which of these four you would dare to claim God lacked. To grasp this more clearly, let each of these virtues, if you please, present its own speech and address, as it were. Let Power say: "After the kingdom of heaven, let us make a wonderful creature in the second rank, so that in the possession of our empire the things that come first may not also seem to be the last. Let us complete this beautiful fabric of the world, so that we may make man in it and set him over it, and through him the world may be ordered, possessed and adorned." Let Goodness say: "It is not right that heavenly beings alone should enjoy our benefits. Let us make man on earth too, so that we may exercise the abundance of our grace toward him, extend the gifts of our kindness to him and pour into him the riches of our innate love." Let Wisdom say: "Let us not only make him but also honour him with a sense of reason and discernment and fill him with the light of prudence. Let us make him simple, and let us make him shrewd: simple, so that he does not cunningly bring about evil, and shrewd, so that he does not fall into it unawares. Let us instil in him a love of good and an understanding of evil, and, in keeping with our governance, let us leave him in the hand of his own counsel and in the freedom of his own judgment."

Meanwhile Power, in which foreknowledge also resides, deliberates with itself: "What are we to do? If we leave him free to his own choice, we foreknow that he will stray into the byways of sin. We foresee that he will turn the gifts of his precious making into instruments of wickedness. So if we want our work in him to last forever, let us take sin out of his power." Justice says: "Not so. It does not suit our laws that one who must be proved by opposition should be unable to show what he is by his own strength. It does not suit our laws, I say, that we should deny the material and cause of glory to one whom we wish to be glorified through his own service as well. Nor does it suit them that we should make one whom we desire to reward by bare grace earn nothing by his own labour. Rather, let these allied and sister virtues act in him one by one and play their parts. Let it belong to Power to create him exalted among all visible things, though he is to live especially among enemies. Let it belong to Wisdom to order him to be prudent, to Goodness to help him as he strives, and to Justice to crown him as victor."

"Let us therefore make man, for his own benefit and for our dignity, such that not necessity but will draws him to the right side. Let him understand evil by reason and accomplish good by virtue. Let us make him such that goodness is in his nature, while wickedness is outside his nature. Let him have the good in his will and evil in his power. Let him will the good by nature and be able to do evil in act. Let him keep our commandments willingly and be unable to be endangered against his will. For him the first ground for praise will be that he both can sin and does not want to. It is enough that among the four-footed beasts and the brutes, which are to be subject to man, we have already made an animal of this kind: since it is not liable to guilt, it cannot have the fruit of righteousness. But the one to whom we are going to entrust the dignity of our image ought not to resemble cattle. Let us ask the things we formed knowing nothing of sin and ignorant of reason, without any honour of prudence. Will its simplicity profit the beast, or its fruitfulness the tree? In the case of our man, we shall not be able to award the palm of praise if we want his nature to be the slave of necessity."

"He is subject by his condition, free by his discernment and complete in reason. It is therefore right for us to place him under a granted power and a set law, so that keeping the commandment may be the way in to the reward and its cause. For if he has neither the means nor the freedom to do evil, he will have no glory in doing good. If he keeps a praiseworthy soundness only through our kindness and not also through his own effort and labour, it will not be innocence but inertia. Besides, the reward is lost where merit does not come first. He who does not know how to acquire our good things cannot keep them. Unless devoted obedience has come first, the offer of grace becomes cheap. At the same time, it shames the one who rewards if the idle are honoured and the slothful rewarded. Rather, with our help working alongside him, let him become worthy by his own work as well, and let him be happy with a good conscience. For unless the giver's generosity is just, the receiver's happiness will not be complete. And unless the eagerness of the seeker has first been tested, what will the kindness of the giver have to delight in?"

Foreknowledge still debates with Justice and says: "It is better that the human race should not be made at all than that it should be seen to be made only to perish." Goodness and Justice answer: "Not so. Because of the impious Cain, shall the pious Abel not exist? Because of growing wickedness, shall the world not see the righteousness of Noah? Because of Judas, shall we not have Peter? Some will be overcome by the allurements of vice. Because of them, shall those not come into life who are to be crowned by just judgment for the unbending greatness of soul of their austere virtue? Because of the multitude of transgressors, shall the ages of the righteous, the thousands of martyrs and the kingdom of the saints be passed over and left as nothing? Because of those whom we foreknow will sin by their own fault, shall we not make those whom we foreknow will please us by their own merit too? If so, wickedness foreknown will rob our power more than wickedness carried out will harm it. The foreknown generation of the wicked would harm the good, who would then not be created on its account, whereas once created it could at some point have harmed only itself." Then let Goodness say: "Let us make the human race such that it cannot sin." Circumspect Justice replies on the other side: "How shall we give to earthly beings what we have not granted to heavenly ones? How shall human frailty have what the nature of angels did not obtain?" This being so, let the creature not dare to dispute about the Creator's work. It belonged to Power, then, to found man as immortal out of nothing, to Wisdom to make him capable of reason, to Goodness to prepare him for blessedness, and to Justice not to choose him before testing him.

But meanwhile someone persists and says: "If it is certain that sinners will be handed over to punishment in that age and consigned to eternal fire, man ought to have been made in such a way that he could not sin at all." Why do you run ahead of your Author's arrangements, O man? Why do you seek the substance of immortality in the region of death? Why do you seek during the campaign what is being prepared in glory? Why do you demand, before your labour is completed, what has been prepared for after your labour? This will be given, but to one who has already been justified for eternity, when what has been bestowed can no longer be lost. This will be given, but in the time of blessedness. Then there will no longer be any need to conquer sin, or even to know it. Then there will be neither the will nor the possibility to sin. Then living holily, wholly and devoutly will not be a matter of diligence or effort but of nature. This is how divine mercy and justice arrange it, so that whoever has striven for integrity here can no longer be corrupted there by any stain. For God will judge it fitting that the man who refused to sin when he was weak should be unable to sin when he is eternal. Through the ages that roll on without end, there will be joy without fear, reward without envy and a kingdom without an enemy.
FRAGMENTS BELONGING TO THE GAPS IN THE BOOKS ON GRACE
I.

These words come from the end of chapter 14 of the first book On Grace, which is defective. John Maxentius quotes them in the little work entitled "Response to the Letter of Hormisdas" (Migne, Patrologia Graeca 86.1, p. 109; compare what we have set out in the book "Studien über die Schriften des Bischofes von Reii Faustus," p. 22 f.):

"Again, in chapter 15 of the same book, he (that is, Faustus) argues against those who maintain that the gift of believing is not general but special. Among other things he says: 'But you say that it is not given to all, that belief is a personal gift, and that only those whom God has specially granted to believe are able to believe. Not so. For when the Lord demands belief even from unbelievers, he shows that it has been implanted in all. And who is unable to believe even by the very law of nature, when even the demons believe and tremble?'"
II.

In the same place, Maxentius (Migne, loc. cit., p. 111) seems to be referring to chapter 11 of Faustus' second book On Grace, which is today largely lost, when he says (compare what we have set out in the book cited above, p. 23 f.):

"Hence also in the eleventh chapter of the second book he (that is, Faustus) shamelessly and brazenly asserts the following about many people who lived not only before the Lord's coming but even before the law of the letter. He claims that by their natural strength, without the help of grace, they were saved, reached full purity of heart and perfect righteousness, and deserved to become sons of God."
